title: Shaw and Some Contemporaries (Who's Afraid of Bernard Shaw? Some Personalities in Shaw's Plays by Stanley Weintraub)
abstract: The final essay on Virginia Woolf in this collection gives rise to the book's title and is also an allusive nod to Edward Albee's 1962 play, whose key phrase, Martha's “Truth and illusion, George; you don't know the difference” (Act 3), is all the more ironic because George is a history professor. Allusions and sources are central concerns of Stanley Weintraub's book that also raises the ancillary consideration of how dramatists generate their ideas. Are they like Autolycus, that “snapper-up of unconsidered trifles”? Do they simply follow popular theatrical trends or perhaps view themselves as furthering a particular movement such as, say, expressionism, absurdism, or whatever? Martin Meisel's Shaw and the Nineteenth-Century Theater (1963) provided one extensive answer about where Shaw turned for his ideas. Now Weintraub applies his vast knowledge of Shaw (and much else) to demonstrating how Shaw, the historian, converted various historical and contemporary figures into theatrical illusions. Moreover, Weintraub enlarges on some literary influences on Shaw and on Shaw's own influence on two dramatists.Beginning appropriately enough with God, the first essay discusses Shaw's “Passion Play” fragment and Shaw's emphasis on Judas's influence on Jesus, a realist/idealist relationship that recurred in later plays. Weintraub points out direct biblical allusions and influences, and draws parallels between Jesus and his mother and Shaw and his mother. Religion is important too in Caesar and Cleopatra, which Weintraub shows to be thoroughly Victorian in its content: “We are in 48 B.C., in mid-Victorian England,” a Bible-familiar England that found Egypt appealing through cheap color lithographs, such as Israel in Egypt (1867), by the painter Edward Poynter (26). Shaw was also deliberate in his attempt “to lure established players for box-office reasons,” such as the highly popular Johnston Forbes-Robertson, who indeed became the Caesar of both the New York and London premieres. In passing, Weintraub notes Shaw's use of the metatheatrical technique of making an audience aware of itself, while acknowledging Shakespeare's earlier use of the device in, for example, Henry V.Shaw was more blatant in borrowing from Schiller's Die Räuber for the “Don Juan in Hell” episode, and from Albany de Fonblanque's biography of General Burgoyne, the latter in an unused 1930 film script for The Devil's Disciple. In the script, Shaw introduces George III's secretary for America, Lord George Germain. More political personalities are dealt with in the “Disraeli in Shaw” essay; indeed, Disraeli emerges as almost omnipresent, being alluded to in The Apple Cart, On the Rocks, Caesar and Cleopatra, The Man of Destiny, Captain Brassbound's Conversion, You Never Can Tell, Man and Superman, and Major Barbara. Additionally, Weintraub credits the last line of Arms and the Man to Disraeli, although this seems to me less persuasive because it appears the line was not spoken in the first production, and subsequently Shaw kept revising the line.Contemporary personalities occupy the remaining 150 pages, the first being the Zulu chief Cetewayo, who visited London in 1882. Shaw incorporated him into Cashel Byron's Profession, and Cetewayo made another appearance in the second scene of The Admirable Bashville. Shaw's love of music emerges in his relationship with Edward Elgar, a somewhat curious acquaintanceship since Elgar was a Tory. Much of the relationship seems incidental, however, although Weintraub does connect Elgar to Back to Methuselah and The Simpleton of the Unexpected Isles. Lady Colin Campbell could not have been more dissimilar to Elgar, as the details of her scandalous life and divorce reveal. On Shaw's recommendation, she took over his art column for the Star in 1889, and Weintraub reveals her influence on the composition of The Philanderer. That there was something of her in Ann Whitefield is a stretch, as Weintraub admits. The artist Kathleen Scott is treated to a short biography in which Shaw plays but a tangential role. However, Weintraub finds traces of her in Misalliance and Back to Methuselah but confesses these are “only the smallest of hints, perhaps” (125).Reverse influence is the theme of the essays on Eugene O'Neill and Noël Coward. O'Neill and Shaw never met, even when O'Neill visited London in 1928. Nevertheless, O'Neill identified with Marchbanks in Candida: “In a romantic exchange with one young woman, O'Neill implored her, ‘I make the poet's plea in Candida’” (141). O'Neill integrated Marchbanks into his autobiographical Richard of Ah, Wilderness! Caesar and Cleopatra influenced Marco's Millions quite extensively, as Weintraub's close reading and evidence demonstrate. The young Noël Coward plagiarized You Never Can Tell in The Young Idea (1922) and, rather than incurring his ire, Shaw wrote and encouraged Coward in pursuing his career. Similar advice followed when Coward fell afoul of financial restrictions in World War II.Just how convoluted influences and indebtedness can be emerges in the essay on Edward VIII's abdication, The Apple Cart, and Shaw's playlet The King, the Constitution and the Lady (the latter is reproduced extensively). Shaw thought Edward should do as he pleased (in the matter of Mrs. Simpson) much as The Apple Cart had argued for King Magnus, and as the new playlet proposed, to the delight of Winston Churchill. However, Edward, Churchill, and Shaw were on the losing side, as a contemporary nautical joke illustrated: “The king, who by his position had also been Admiral of the Fleet, had now settled on becoming ‘the third mate on an American tramp’” (187).And so to Virginia Woolf, who, with her husband, was at the weekend with the Webbs when Shaw was working on Heartbreak House and into which some of the visitors were incorporated. Thereafter, Virginia and Shaw made infrequent contact, as their personalities were quite different; moreover, Virginia thought poets far more important than dramatists such as Shaw. Nevertheless, Weintraub winkles out Shavian echoes in The Voyage Out (influenced by Mrs Warren) and Mrs. Dalloway (The Doctor's Dilemma).I detected one or two Homeric nods. The dates on British theatrical censorship vary throughout the book, although eventually the correct 1968 is settled on. Arms and the Man was produced in 1894, not 1895 (30), and it is not true that 1902 marked the end of Elgar's music for the theater (79). But in the midst of such encyclopedic knowledge, this is hardly amiss. Moreover, in leading us through this amazing wealth of connections, allusions, relationships, and influences, Weintraub never falters in his lucid writing that captures the reader's interest and fascination.

title: Majstor mirenja, spajanja i kombiniranja suprotnosti
abstract: Igor Rončević has been painting for a very long time with the consciousness that his painterly signature can be constructed from a series of disparate fragments, and so his collage paintings are composed of elements or stylistic details thanks to which his canvas has become a place where ambivalent worlds meet - an ntersection of their paths. Rončević is therefore, a painter of ludic individualism, but, at the same time, painter with wide erudition and above all, a curious pirit, who, in a unique way - in different clusters of itations - applies and joins together experiences from he entire history of art. In his works we have for some ime observed the meetings of some of at first sight rreconcilable contrasts - the experiences of Pop art, European and American abstraction, experiences of gestural and lyrical provenance, different traces and tyles of figuration... All this heterogeneous material has been relativized in his interpretation, often even in blasphemous combinations; in a conspicuously easy and organic way, these combinations merge into a unique whole consisting of forms and meanings which are difficult to decipher. Analysis of Rončević’s paintings reveals the absence of a specific rational system that accumulates the building blocks of a painting - a mental landscape - but not the absence of a peculiar talent for creating compositional balance in a painting.The basic building block in the cycle Dulčić’s fragments is the line - stripes, that is linear, ribbon-like shapes, curved lines which meander on the surface of the canvas, and in the painted area, lines freely applied with a finger in fresh paint. The basic ludic element is colour, and the cartography of the canvas is a road with innumerable directions. The painter, treating the surface of the canvas as a field of total action, creates networks of interlacing multicoloured verticals, lively blue, blue-green and brown hues, coloured without an apparent system or principle, and also of varying width but, despite the seemingly limited starting points of his painting, he creates situations rich in interesting shifts and intriguing pictorial and colouristic happenings. The painter’s main preoccupation is the interaction of ‘neon’ colours (obviously a reference to the twentieth-century’s ‘neon’ enthusiasts), which has been achieved with a simple composition consisting of a knot of interwoven ribbons of intense colours which belong to a different chromatic register in each painting. Streams of complementary or contrasting colours, which spread out across the painted field like the tributaries of a river, subject to confluence, adopting features of the neighbouring colour, sharing the light and darkness of a ‘neon’. Although the impression implies the opposite, the application of colours, their touching and eventual interaction are strictly controlled by the skill of a great colourist. Dulčić’s fragments display Rončević’s fascinating power of unexpected associative perception. The painter now reaches for the excess of colour remaining on his palette from the work on previous paintings. He applies the colour to the canvas with a spatula in a relief impasto, and he revives the dried background with a lazure glaze of a chosen colour. On a saturated but still obviously ‘neon’ grid, the painter - evenly, like a collage detail - applies islands of open colour on the surface of the painting, which he finally paints with a brush, applying vertical white lines over the colour. These shapes of an associative and metaphorical nature are an integral part of the semantic scaffolding of composition but, without particular declarative frameworks and associative attributes, we can never precisely say what they actually represent although they are reminiscent of many things, such as seeds, bacteria, cellular microcosm, unstable primitive forms of life, the macrocosm of the universe, the structures of crystals, technical graphs, calligraphy, secret codes... The linear clarity of the drawing makes motifs concrete and palpable, possessing volume, in fact, possessing bulging physicality. In new paintings, the personal sign of the artist, which arrived in the painting from the activity of the conscious and the unconscious, has been replaced with small shapes, most similar to an oval, which look like separate pieces attached to the surface of the painting and which are reminiscent of specific painterly and artistic tendencies. Their monochrome surfaces are filled with verticals which are particles of the rational or, to put it better, from the constructivist stylistic repertoire, reminiscent, for example, of Daniel Buren’s verticals. Two divergent components - the abstract and the rational - stylistically and typologically separate, but chronologically parallel - pour into an evocative encounter which reveals a nostalgia towards two-dimensional painting. Experiences of posters and graphic design, gestural abstraction, abstract expressionism, lyrical abstraction and everything else that can be observed in this cycle of paintings are a homage to global modern painting, while the islands on the paintings pay tribute to the constructivist section of the twentieth-century avant-garde. The contents of Rončević’s paintings are also reminiscent of the rhythmicality of human figures in Dulčić’s representations of the events on Stradun, town squares, beaches, dances... In addition, to Rončević, as a Mediterranean man - in his formative years - Dulčić was an important painter and, if we persist in searching for formal similarities in their ‘handwritings’, we will find them in the hedonism of painterly matter and the sensuality of colour, luxuriant layers, the saturation of impasto painting, gestural vitality, but mostly in the Mediterranean sensibility, the Mediterranean sonority of colour, their solarity, the southern light and virtuosity of their metiérs. Like Dulčić, Rončević is also re-confirmed as a painter of impulses, of lush, luscious and extremely personalized matter, of layers of pigments, of vehement and moveable gestures, of fluid pictorialism…* * *Let us also say in conclusion that Rončević does not want to state, establish or interpret anything but to incessantly reveal possibilities, their fundamental interchangeability and arbitrariness, and following that, a general insecurity. With the skill of an experienced master painter, he also questions relationships with eclecticism and the aesthetics of kitsch; for example, he explores how far a painter can go into ornamentalization, decorativeness and coquetry without falling into the trap of kitsch but to maintain regularly the classy independence of a multilayered artifact and to question the very stamina of painting. He persistently reveals loyalty to the traditional medium of painting, the virtuosity of his métier and a strong individual stamp, strengthening his own position as a peculiar and outstandingly cultivated painter, but he also exhibits the inventiveness which makes him both different and recognizable in a series of similar painting adventures.

title: Formal affinities of architecture of the "white city" in Tel Aviv
abstract: S t r e s z c z e n i e Celem pracy jest przedstawienie wplywu, jaki wywarly na urbanistyczną i architektoniczną forme miasta Tel Awiw (Izrael) awangardowe trendy w europejskiej architekturze trzeciej dekady XX w. Praca oparta jest na badaniach prowadzonych na miejscu oraz na publikacjach omawiających nurty wystepujące w ramach Stylu Miedzynarodowego w Europie i w Izraelu. Wynik pracy jest istotny dla szczegolowej wiedzy o architekturze miasta budowanego od podstaw pod wplywem Szkoly Architektury Bauhaus i idei Le Corbusiera, przenikanych dynamiką architektonicznego ekspresjonizmu. W latach trzydziestych, ze wzgledu na sytuacje polityczną Europy, skrzyzowanie nurtow architektury znalazlo sie wlaśnie tam, po przybyciu z Europy mlodych architektow zydowskiego pochodzenia, szukających schronienia w Palestynie. Wyksztalceni byli w roznych uczelniach i rozne mieli doświadczenia zawodowe. Tel Awiw byl dla nich poligonem doświadczalnym rozwiązan mających na celu adaptacje Stylu Miedzynarodowego do nowych warunkow geograficznych i klimatycznych. Temat ten, jak dotąd jest nieobecny w toczącej sie wspolcześnie dyskusji na temat architektury modernizmu w Polsce, mimo ze urodzeni i wyksztalceni w Polsce architekci brali udzial, jeśli nie udzial wazny, w tym procesie. K e y w o r d s : Tel Aviv; Modern Movement and International Style; Bauhaus; Expressionism; Jewish architects from European countries; Adaptation to the local conditions; Architects educated in Poland. 2/2010 A R C H I T E C T U R E C I V I L E N G I N E E R I N G E N V I R O N M E N T 15 A R C H I T E C T U R E C I V I L E N G I N E E R I N G E N V I R O N M E N T The Si les ian Univers i ty of Technology No. 2/2010 T . B a r d z i n s k a B o n e n b e r g (Christian) countries. Throughout the centuries the two groups developed different cultures which met in the 20th century in Palestine, and later, since 1948 in Israel. Zionism, a new ideology, developed among European Jews at the break of the 20th century, spread across Europe causing, in the late twentieth century first waves of migration from Eastern Europe to the historical land. Sandy sea shore dunes adjoining Jaffa were difficult for settling in. The beginning of modern Tel Aviv was initiated by construction of New Tzedek, which between 1887-1896 became a first settlement outside Jaffa built by Ashkenazi immigrants. “Newe Tzedek” is characterized by simple, two-storey buildings constructed of local sandstone. Early architecture of Tel Aviv-to-be consisted largely of oneor two-storey houses: from simple “cubes” to a variety of styles popular in those days in European architecture. Second wave of immigrants in the first years of the 20th century resulted in decision upon a complex plan for a new suburb. Jewish community has bought 5 hectares of sand dunes to the north of Jaffa planning to organize a comfortable, healthy and modern place for living. The settlers were Zionists, adherents of socialist ideology, basically from Poland and Russia. In 1909, sixty six families bought and parceled the land, giving names to first delimited streets and building first houses of the city that was named Tel Aviv one year later. However, at the same time, in Europe a Modern Movement trend germinated and gradually gained supporters among artists and young architects. In the thirties, particularly when the Nazis were gaining power in Germany, Jewish citizens fled the country and gradually whole Europe. Many of them settled in Palestine. At that time the land was under British Mandate, a result of the Paris Peace Conference in 1919, with assumption that Jewish state will be established there. In the following years population of Tel Aviv rose from 550 residents in 1909 to 40 000 in 1926 and 150 000 in 1937. [1] This situation was generated by the course of events that took place in Europe. Inevitable urban expansion created a challenge for architects. Many of them, Jews by birth, educated in the Bauhaus School of Architecture and in other leading European architectonic schools arrived in Palestine and established their practices there, bringing the ideas of International Style with them. Tel Aviv’s city centre urban layout was delimited in 1925. Today it is the only full realization of the idea of a Garden City conceived by Patrick Geddes, who was commissioned to prepare the plan of the city. He took advantage of the city’s topographic situation planning the grid of streets with a goal to employ the sea breeze to ventilate the housing area. [1] In Tel Aviv the ideology, design and texture of the International Style buildings were carried out in a manner never repeated elsewhere. Geddes’s layout envisaged houses built on small, individual, private plots, which, as a matter of fact, contradicted socialistic ideas of Palestinian leaders. 16 A R C H I T E C T U R E C I V I L E N G I N E E R I N G E N V I R O N M E N T 2/2010 Figure 1. Sir Patrick Geddes plan for the new city of Tel Aviv 1925, source: www.telavivarchitecture.com/Tours.html F O R M A L A F F I N I T I E S O F A R C H I T E C T U R E O F T H E “ W H I T E C I T Y ” I N T E L AV I V This problem was solved by building multi flat houses with common areas for the tenants. On the other hand, social ideas were expressed in an exemplary way in cooperative settlements designed within the city for groups of workers; Bauhaus “siedlungs” were their predecessors. [2]

title: Sunshine
abstract: Sunshine is a graphic novel about the problem of memory. The protagonist, Geraldine, is trying to tell her life story, only to find that she cannot discern fact from fiction with certainty; she recalls dreams, lies, family secrets, incidents that are half-remembered or that have been embellished over time, and a close childhood friend who may or may not have existed. Geraldine is primarily occupied with one event, the year she spent in a preventorium, a type of tubercular hospital for children. Her memories from that year are so peculiar that she feels almost convinced she made them up. Preventoriums, now an all-but-forgotten chapter in the history of American medicine, existed from 1909 to 1970 and were designed to combine "the best elements of a school, sanatorium, and middle-class American home" (Connolly, 54). Children deemed at-risk for tuberculosis--typically the children of working-class or immigrant families--were sent to stay in these institutions. There they received nutritious food, fresh air, and instruction on proper hygiene. Their education also tended to include a heavy emphasis on middle-class Protestant values. My maternal grandfather, Chandler Franks, stayed in the Magee, Mississippi Preventorium in from 1929 to 1930. His stories from that period were the original inspiration for Sunshine. I have since interviewed and read memoirs by other former residents of the Magee facility. The events that take place in Sunshine, however, are fictional; for the most part, I have used interview material only to add verisimilitude and sensory detail. Neither Geraldine's home town of Green Pond, Florida, nor the Sea Haven Preventorium where she is sent, bears any resemblance to real places. Geraldine's struggle to reconstruct her past begins when she tries to start drawing her dreams in a journal. Several panels show Geraldine drawing events that occur later in the novel, complicating the reader's experience with the text. Some panels show only her hand holding a pencil, from the same perspective as if the reader were looking down at his or her own hand, putting the reader in Geraldine's position. Geraldine's story is sometimes humorous, sometimes horrific. The combination of humorous and gothic elements draws inspiration from the work of Kelly Link and more recently from Florida State University's "Cute & Creepy" exhibition. Link's stories are often funny and unnerving at the same time "The Specialist's Hat," my favorite in the collection, involves two young girls who are menaced by a grotesque, living hat that once belonged to a magician. The hat is both terrifying and ridiculous. Similarly, the works included in the "Cute & Creepy" show combine images of death and decay with elements such as cartoon animals, flowers, smiling children, and toys. Humor and horror are two sides of the same coin, both stemming from the irrational, and when both are present in the same work, each intensifies the other. The aesthetic of Sunshine combines the cute and the creepy. Geraldine confronts ghosts from her past--both literal and figurative--while also putting up with her sister's irksome obsession with self-help literature. The drawings, which I have rendered in soft graphite, are both gloomy and comical. Some graphic novels that inform my own project include Sloth by Gilbert Hernandez, Black Hole by Charles Burns, and Persepolis by Marjane Satrapi. All three feature stark, black and white drawings, each story makes heavy use of surreal imagery, childhood memories, and dream sequences. In Sloth, a teenager named Miguel Serra wills himself into a coma. When he wakes up, he struggles to rejoin the real world and becomes obsessed with investigating a haunted lemon orchard. Black Hole borrows tropes from black and white B horror movies to tell its story. In it, a sexually-transmitted plague is causing horrific mutations in teenagers all over America. They begin growing horns, tails, fur, or extra body parts. Those affected are forced to live in the woods, away from society--an apt metaphor for teenage alienation. Sloth and Black Hole helped inspire the writing of Sunshine because of their nuanced exploration of the unconscious. Persepolis, Satrapi's memoir of growing up in Iran during the Islamist Revolution, is a work of nonfiction, but it was still instrumental in shaping my original concept for Sunshine, since it takes the form of a memoir in places. I also admire Satrapi's drawing style, which recalls German expressionism. The graphic novel is the ideal genre for this story because of its liminality. Comics are neither a wholly visual nor wholly literary art form, but something in between; the boundaries between visual art and literature are blurred. As David Carrier writes in The Aesthetics of Comics, "We expect the world to fit our preconceived stable categories, and so what falls in between is easily felt, depending upon our temperament and politics, to be either exciting or menacing. Hence the fascination with, and fear of, cross-dressing, androgyny, people of `mixed-race,' comics, and other forms of in-betweenness" (70-71). In Sunshine, the instability of the art form mirrors the instability of the narration. The boundaries between fact and fiction, horror and humor, are blurred, and Geraldine's story happens in the margins, in the white space between panels. The graphic novel also offers a more complex mode of storytelling. Hélène Cixous writes, "I would like to write like a painter. I would like to write like painting" (104). Cixous refers to the immediacy offered by visual media. The viewer absorbs an image before having the chance to apply any other filters to it. Or, as Alain Robbe-Grillet explains, "In this future universe of the novel, gestures and objects will be there before being something" (21). In a graphic novel, images exist in the reader's mind before they signify anything else. As the reader takes the images together with the written text, the objects on the page begin to give way to ideas, but "only provisionally, and [they] will accept the tyranny of significations only in appearance--derisively, one might say--the better to show how alien they remain to man" (Robbe-Grillet, 22). I believe that the graphic novel is the perfect example of the "new novel" the Robbe-Grillet was searching for. It simultaneously creates a solid world of objects and people and an ephemeral world of ideas. By using this form, I hope to tell a story whose images will lodge in the reader's mind long after the novel has ended.

title: Art at the Time of Turmoil: Max Beckmann
abstract: Weimar Republic is the name applied to Germany as it emerged from World War I. The 1918 armistice amounted to Germany's defeat. The German emperor Wilhelm II was forced to abdicate and the Weimar Republic was proclaimed on November 9, 1918. A series of violent crises followed, and for a few years the country veered from one political extreme to another. On the one hand, a very short-lived Bavarian Soviet Republic was declared in Munich in 1921; on the other hand, there was the unsuccessful so-called Beer Hall Putsch led by Hitler in 1923. In the background, there was economic collapse and extreme hyperinflation between 1920 and 1923. In 1920, the Nazi party emerged. Later, the Social Democrats managed to stabilize the politics somewhat. The economy also improved following the 1924 Dawes Plan, which involved American finance. Another financial rescue measure, the Young Plan, was negotiated in 1929 but the Wall Street Crash derailed it, profoundly affecting Germany. Hitler became chancellor in 1933, and the Nazis very quickly dismantled the Weimar democracy (1, 2). The relatively stable period from 1924 to 1929 is regarded as the golden era of the Weimar culture. There was a momentary flourishing of literature, cinema, theatre, music, and philosophy. Edmund Husserl (1859–1938) developed phenomenology, and Martin Heidegger (1889–1976), who was influenced by Husserl, published his influential Being and Time in 1927, elaborating existentialism (3, 4). The Frankfurt School of Philosophy, founded in 1923 and influential to this day, originally centered around the Institute for Social Research at Goethe University in Frankfurt. Inevitably, the brutality and horrors of the past war cast a shadow over all intellectual pursuits. As far as science was concerned, there was a backlash towards scientific determinism. The so-called Lebensphilosophie (the philosophy of life), with its rejection of reductionism, gained ground. In the arts there was increased emphasis on the spiritual and irrational, curiously parallel to the interest in the applied arts, the Bauhaus concept being a prominent example. The Dada movement, which was emerging in Zurich, Paris, Berlin, Cologne, and New York, attempted to redefine art in view of the cultural catastrophe of the war. In the early years of the Republic, the visual arts were strongly influenced by Expressionism. Around 1920, a new movement appeared, which became known as the Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity). Its proponents rejected the Expressionists' emphasis on emotion and focused on the objective presentation of reality, however unpalatable. Artists linked with New Objectivity include Käthe Kollwitz (1867–1945), Otto Dix (1891–1969), George Grosz (1893–1959), Christian Schad (1894–1982), and Max Beckmann (5). The intellectual turmoil extended to science. It was the time of quick development of atomic physics. Albert Einstein (1879–1955) and other prominent physicists and mathematicians worked in Germany at the time. Einstein was born in Ulm and was appointed Director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Physical Institute and Professor at the University of Berlin in 1914. He held these posts until he emigrated to the US in 1933 (6). In 1971, the historian Paul Forman examined the reaction of scientists, particularly physicists and mathematicians, to what he called an environment hostile to scientific rationalism. He proposed that this social pressure made the scientists make conceptual concessions, softening their attitude toward causality in science. The key tenet of the Forman hypothesis was that this modified intellectual framework contributed to the development of probability-based concepts, essential in the formulation of quantum mechanics (7). The life of the artist Max Beckmann was representative of the period because it spanned two world wars (8, 9). Beckmann was born in Leipzig and trained at the Weimar-Saxon Grand Ducal Academy in Weimar. In the early years of his career, he visited Paris, and from 1904 to 1916 he lived in Berlin. At the beginning of World War I, Beckmann supported the war. He volunteered as a medical officer and was at Ypres in Belgium in 1915. He became increasingly shocked by what he saw; in 1915, he was discharged because of “physical and mental exhaustion.” After the war, he settled in Frankfurt, where he taught at the Städel Art School. He was dismissed from the school in 1933 and moved back to Berlin. He finally left Germany in July, 1937. He spent the 1938–39 winter in Paris and then moved to Amsterdam, where he stayed throughout World War II. Like many others, he kept trying to emigrate to the US. He eventually arrived in the US in 1947. From 1947 to 1949, he held a nonpermanent position at the School of Fine Arts at Washington University in St. Louis, MO. In 1949, he moved to the Brooklyn Museum Art School and began teaching in 1950. During the summers of 1949 and 1950, he taught at the University of Colorado in Boulder and at Mills College in Oakland, respectively. Beckmann died in the US in 1951. Initially Max Beckman was peripherally associated with the German Expressionists. Later, he was regarded as a prominent member of the Berlin Secession, and he exhibited with this movement in 1906. In 1918, he became one of the leaders of New Objectivity. Beckmann produced works that mixed reality with myths and dreams. They contained symbolism and allegories, although the artist was not keen on explaining their meaning. He adopted the form of triptych, based on the medieval three-panel paintings often used on altars. The Departure, shown in Fig. 1, was his first triptych painting, which he created after being dismissed from the post in Frankfurt (10). Another triptych, Carnival, is now at the University of Iowa (11). Frankfurt 1932, Berlin 1933–35. Oil on canvas, three panels, side panels 7′ 3/4″ × 39 1/4″ (215.3 × 99.7 cm), center panel 7′ 3/4″ × 45 3/8″ (215.3 × 115.2 cm). Given anonymously (by exchange). Digital Image © The Museum of Modern Art/Licensed by SCALA / Art Resource, NY. © 2017 Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York/VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn. Reproduced with permission. Beckmann also created about 85 self-portraits. A large collection of his works is contained at the St. Louis Art Museum (12). His oeuvre is placed somewhere between realism and abstraction. Importantly, although he was strongly aware of space and form, he also paid attention to the two-dimensional surface of the canvas, which makes him one of the precursors of later art movements that focused on two dimensions. Beckmann belongs to artists–intellectuals. He was well read and wrote throughout his life, providing invaluable insight into his personality (9). He was deeply interested in past masters and regarded Cézanne particularly highly. He was also influenced by Courbet, the Impressionists, and by van Gogh and Munch. Interestingly, he was critical of Gauguin and particularly of Matisse, and he was strongly opposed to abstract painting. The instability, turmoil, and horrors of war and persecution are never far from Beckmann's art. At the same time, his life is a testimony to an extraordinary phenomenon seen both in arts and science throughout the ages: whatever the violence and however unhinged the politics, there are both scientists and artists who still manage to pursue their intellectual vocation and through this preserve continuity of culture.

title: Cumulation, Revolution, and Progress
abstract: expressionism, pop art, op art, abstract geometry . . . Perhaps painting in each of these paradigms (if we may call them that) achieves progress by cumulation, but painting does not. As Kuhn points out,7 painting was once the model of progress by cumulation. Any good history of the subject records how, just as a science increases its explanatory and predictive power, painting increased its representational: by the invention of perspective technique, for instance, and of impressionist. But progress in painting did not survive the revolution that overthrew the representational paradigm. For this revolution did not replace the old paradigm with a new one, as any scientific revolution does, but retained the old one while taking on a multitude of new ones rivaling the old and one another. Perhaps each of these achieves progress by cumulation, but painting does not. Or think of religion. There was always a multitude of religions: Shintoism, Judaism, Islam, Eastern Orthodoxy, Roman Catholicism, and so on. Until fairly recent times, however, there seem not to have been rival religions, religions competing in the same market or for the same audience. Doubtless there was, by  criterion of progress, progress by cumulation in Roman Catholicism. But the Reformation, like the revolution that overthrew the representational paradigm in painting, retained the old paradigm while taking on new ones rivaling it and one another. Sectarian progress is still possible, but not religious. Perhaps literary criticism achieved  progress by cumulation through the eighteenth century. The concept of literature as imitation was at least a germ of a paradigm, and in one way or another most critics developed it until well into that century. In using it to discrimi7 Structure, pp. 161-62. Like representational painting and Roman Catholicism, imitation has survived revolutions. Among its rivals-notably the romantic or expressive paradigm (relating literature to writers' genius, intentions, imaginations, feelings, emotions, minds, sincerity, and so forth) and the objective (the autonomous work) 8-imitation lives on and, as we shall see, not just in the pages of book-review supplements. With literary criticism as with painting and religion, the existence of rival paradigms precludes progress in the activity as a whole whether by cumulation or by cumulation and revolution. Some of the rival paradigms, however, look like paradigms in normal science, and in them there is something that looks like progress by cumulation in normal science. The New Criticism (the one christened by Ransom, not by Spingarn), for example, has  of the marks of a scientific paradigm. It has a theory or family of theories: that literature is autonomous (hence the intentional and the affective fallacies), that the essence of literature is linguistic (there is a language of poetry), that literature is organic (hence the inseparability of form and content, and the heresy of paraphrase), that every work is symbolic (has a dramatized, not stated, theme), and so on. It has a procedure for application of the theory: close reading or explication of texts. And critics working in the paradigm learn the theory and the procedure less by studying statements of them than by imitating examples of application of the theory. What is more, they constitute a mystery of professors and students who are the sole arbiters of one another's work and (apart from unpledged undergraduates on their way to law, business, medicine, or home economics) the sole audience for it. They achieve progress by cumulation through applying the theory to particular works: first to the more amenable (metaphysical and modern poetry), then to the recalcitrant (medieval, eighteenth-century, and Victorian poetry; drama; prose fiction). The fruit of these applications is usually new readings or revaluations. There are, however,  significant differences between this criticism and normal science. For one thing, the New Criticism has no single aim. If this criticism were normal science, the critic would ask himself what phenomena 8 For an account of these paradigms, see M. H. Abrams, The Mirror and the Lamp (New York, 1953), Ch. i. Composing, interpreting, and evaluating literature are, he would doubtless note, human activities, a special case of composing, interpreting, and evaluating discourse; and these activities need explanation. How do people compose poems? Interpret them? Evaluate them? Why? What, if anything, must they know to do these things? How does literature differ from other discourse? New Critics do, indeed, ask questions of this kind, but often they confound them with questions of kinds that a scientist would not ask. Normative questions: How ought people interpret poems? Evaluate them? How does good literature differ from bad? Technological, pedagogical, or political questions: How can interpretative skill be fostered? How can humane studies be revived? How can the tide of relativism be stemmed? In this respect, the New Criticism is not unlike such sciences manque as sociology and political science. Lacking a single aim, they lack a single criterion of progress. A related difference between the New Criticism and normal science is in what constitutes application of a theory-indeed, in what constitutes a theory. In normal science, a theory presupposes the existence of phenomena to be explained; and application of the theory consists in testing it by elaborating and refining it to explain a widening range of related kinds of phenomena and thus realizing its explanatory potential. This is the way that normal science achieves progress by cumulation. In the New Criticism, however, the purpose of application of the theory to particular works is not only or even chiefly to test the theory against a widening range of kinds of literature (as in Brooks's The Well-Wrought Urn) but also either (I) to explain or (2) to interpret or evaluate particular works of literature. Doing (I) consists in showing that a work has the properties that the theory predicts: irony, for example, or a dramatized theme. It is a bit like a physicist's going to a parking lot in subzero weather and inspecting the radiator of a particular car, not to show that water freezes at temperatures below 32 0 F. (testing the theory), but to show that water in that particular radiator has frozen. Doing (2) consists in using the theory to interpret (a new reading) or evaluate (a revaluation) a work. So used, a theory does not presuppose the existence of phenomena to be explained (interpretations, evaluations); the phenomena presuppose the existence of the theory. No theory, no interpretation or evaluation. Though progress by cumulation is possible by doing either (I) or (2), it is not the kind of progress found in normal science.10 Perhaps the most important difference between the New Criticism and normal science is that the former lacks criteria for judging applications of the theory--for deciding between rival readings or evaluations of a given work, for instance. For criteria to exist, the key terms of a theory must be made precise and unambiguous enough that criteria can be invoked. All theories are, as we have seen, vague; and progress by cumulation in normal science depends upon their vagueness: elaborating and refining a scientific theory and thus realizing its explanatory potential is largely a matter of reducing vagueness or eliminating ambiguity. title: Greg Barnhisel, Cold War Modernists: Art, Literature, and American Cultural Diplomacy. New York: Columbia University Press, 2015. 322 pp. $40.00
abstract: A term like “modernism” exudes the sort of elasticity that is bound to attract scholars eager to parse its various meanings, no matter how elusive. An entire journal now exists that is devoted to the classification of modernism and to studies in relevant works of literature in particular. Because the standard experimentalist works emerged at roughly the same time as the rise of fascism and Nazism, modernism ought to be a good candidate to set off against the despotisms of the right. The key episode in this regard was the notorious exhibition of Entartete Kunst (degenerate art) that the Nazis mounted in Munich in 1937. And yet Ezra Pound, a supremely modernist poet (“Make it new!”) who championed T. S. Eliot and James Joyce, broadcast so many dreadful speeches from Fascist Italy that only a clinical diagnosis of his madness spared him from a postwar conviction for treason. That a tyranny of the left, in the Stalinist USSR, also impugned and outlawed modernism, and exalted the style of socialist realism instead, suggests how tempting it is to define modernism—at least in part—by its incompatibility with totalitarianism. Yet, in 1947, when Harry Truman came across Circus Girl Resting, a painting by the Japanese-American Yasuo Kuniyoshi, the president exclaimed: “If this is art, I’m a Hottentot” (p. 55). Perhaps no artistic movement ever provoked so varied a spectrum of political resistance.But in the United States, hostile Fair Dealers like Truman tended to be outnumbered by conservatives, who were typically members of Congress of conventional aesthetic taste, insofar as they thought about the sublimity of painting or music at all. In the name of commonplace opinion and the thrift that taxpayers expected, such foes snapped at a visionary effort in public diplomacy that helped win the Cold War in the art galleries and in the little magazines. Calculations of the throw-weight of missiles were not enough; Abstract Expressionism could be enlisted to defeat Communism as well. What Greg Barnhisel crisply labels “Cold War modernism” constituted a claim that American culture could trump its Soviet counterpart, because the United States promoted individuality of expression and the freedom to be as creative as one's talent might permit. America meant the right to paint a model who has three eyes and a body that could be blocked out into cubes, or to compose a piece of music that may reveal a beginning and middle and end—but not necessarily in that order. Such works demonstrated the autonomy of art in a democratic society at a time when the exemplars of the avant-garde elsewhere were imprisoned and even executed. Ideas are weapons, the liberal columnist Max Lerner had announced in a book by that title in 1939, and the director of the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), the editors of Perspectives USA, and the bureaucrats at the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) shared a willingness to add those weapons to the arsenal of U.S. statecraft during the early phase of the Cold War.The tale that Barnhisel recounts is coherently organized, superbly researched, and judiciously balanced. Cold War Modernism sees nothing sinister in the alliance between cultural institutions and the agencies of government propaganda, personified in Nelson Rockefeller (a president of MoMA who became an assistant secretary of state) and in Archibald MacLeish (a Left Bank poet in the 1920s who two decades later also became an assistant secretary of state). Barnhisel's book also avoids any hint of triumphalism, perhaps because the actual impact of CIA-sponsored journals such as Encounter or the Russian-language magazine Amerika can never be assessed with any precision. Although his chapter on Encounter adds little to the considerable scholarship that has already been devoted to the secret funding and editorial policies of that London-based journal, and although his chapter on James Laughlin's resolutely apolitical Perspectives USA fails to make a convincing case for the “Cold War” part of the advancement of “modernism,” Barnhisel otherwise offers a series of cogent and lucid chapters on particular episodes. These include the distribution of books through the Informational Media Guaranty (IMG), which occasionally had to weigh the eminence of U.S. authors against the controversies their novels generated (whether for obscenity or for leftism), and the mission of the Voice of America, which frequently had to weigh the ideal of reliably accurate reporting against the need to reinforce the aims of U.S. foreign policy.In acknowledging the sophistication of President Dwight D. Eisenhower's public diplomacy, Cold War Modernism amplifies the revisionist view of his administration. He signed into law, for example, the formation of the United States Information Agency. Cultural exchanges with the Soviet Union were also inaugurated during the “Ike Age,” as a thaw could be detected in the cultures of the two adversaries. By the end of the 1950s, the U.S. Department of State no longer enforced the acid-test of fierce anti-Communism so rigidly that works of Ben Shahn, for example, could be denied official exhibition abroad. An irony embedded in the resourceful and popular programs that Barnhisel portrays is that some of them were sponsored under the Smith-Mundt Act of 1948, even though, as the journalist I. F. Stone cracked in in his Polemics and Prophecies in 1969, when a library named for the Republican Senator was opened in his home state of South Dakota, “the only time [Karl] Mundt ever came close to a book was to see whether or not it might have been written by a Red.” Barnhisel also traces how modernism became middle-brow, its bold novelties the stuff of advertisements, its experimentalism enhancing the aesthetic prestige of executive suites. No longer could anyone envision in the postwar United States a sequel to the riot that erupted at a Stravinsky premiere in Paris in 1913; modernism had become domesticated, its claws clipped.When the Department of State decided to send writers abroad to discuss their own works and to ruminate on the state of contemporary fiction, no one could have predicted that the icon of such excursions would be the least cosmopolitan among the galaxy of writers who had achieved fame in the 1920s, a villager who had spent most of life utterly indifferent to politics. Although nearly all of William Faulkner's books had been out of print as late as 1945, the sensational news of a Nobel Prize four years later catapulted him to a plane of international recognition that the Department of State valued. Whether in Brazil or in Italy, whether in Japan or in Iceland, and whether drunk or sober, the author of the grisly story “A Rose for Emily” proved himself to be an engaging representative of American culture. His visits clicked in no small measure because he had never attached himself to causes or coteries, because he lacked any political agenda of his own to advance.Barnhisel nevertheless misses a striking Cold War connection made in Manila in 1955. Speaking there, Faulkner conjectured that even during the current bleak phase in the evolution of Russian writing, successors to Leo Tolstoy and Feodor Dostoyevsky were already describing the excruciating pain of the soul of man under socialism. Even in the USSR, “they right now are writing. … They hide it … then bury it, and someday I think it will appear,” Faulkner predicted. (See Lion in the Garden: Interviews with William Faulkner, 1926–1962, New York, Random House, p. 206.) He could not possibly have known that, while then living in “perpetual exile” in Karaganda, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn was beginning to mount a literary attack that would undermine whatever moral claims the Soviet system could still manage to invoke. One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich, as well as the three volumes of The Gulag Archipelago, still lay ahead, and their impact proved to be incalculable. They vindicated the project of Barnhisel's Cold War modernists that widespread admiration for the values of freedom and individuality gave the West an immense advantage in the struggle for hearts and minds.

title: Simon Shepherd, The Cambridge Introduction to Modern British TheatreThe Cambridge Introduction to Modern British Theatre. Simon Shepherd. Cambridge and New York: Cambridge University Press, 2009. Pp. vii+250.
abstract: Previous articleNext article FreeSimon Shepherd, The Cambridge Introduction to Modern British Theatre The Cambridge Introduction to Modern British Theatre. Simon Shepherd. Cambridge and New York: Cambridge University Press, 2009. Pp. vii+250.John H. MuseJohn H. MuseUniversity of Chicago Search for more articles by this author PDFPDF PLUSFull Text Add to favoritesDownload CitationTrack CitationsPermissionsReprints Share onFacebookTwitterLinked InRedditEmailQR Code SectionsMoreDesigned for classroom use, the Cambridge Introduction series aims to provide students accessible and comprehensive coverage of its topics. Simon Shepherd eschews coverage of cardinal literary figures and moments in modern British theater in favor of multidimensional institutional history, organized thematically into four chapters: where it happens, who does it, what they make, and why they do it. The word “theatre” in the book’s title signals Shepherd’s self-conscious distance from another introduction to this material, Christopher Innes’s Modern British Drama: The Twentieth Century, second edition (Cambridge University Press, 2002). Where Innes focuses primarily on texts written for the London stage and on their canonical, usually white male authors, Shepherd strives to attend to the entire theatrical experience, including its spaces, its range of professional roles and collaborations, its forays into nonrealistic and nontextual performance, and its diverse ideological commitments. The resulting book is both refreshing and potentially disorienting, especially for students with little prior knowledge of the material.The first two chapters offer useful institutional histories of the dispersal of theatrical spaces and roles, respectively. Chapter 1 provides engaging accounts of the century’s financial and emotional investments in theater spaces, the proliferation of stakeholders taking an interest in those spaces, and the mutual development of new theaters and new audiences. Shepherd is nicely attuned to his stories’ ironies. So while he traces the central fault line between commercialism and aesthetic rigor that characterizes the period, he also complicates that narrative by pointing out how, for instance, Hugh Beaumont’s managerial power made possible considerable experimentation at the Lyric Hammersmith (23), or how the National Theatre’s large budget in the 1970s allowed Peter Hall to fund not mere theatricality but “spectacle as irony” (16). Similarly, the very success of efforts by postwar theater artists to abandon established theater buildings in favor of alternative or derelict spaces had the effect over time of converting some purpose-built theaters into neglected spaces newly worthy of creative attention precisely because they had lost their purpose (58–59). The second chapter, focusing on the roles that shaped theatrical production, highlights similar tensions: nonhierarchical theater collectives ironically fostered the rise of auteur directors; as actor training became more formalized, there was increasing interest in amateur performers and nonmimetic activism; and the rise of ensembles like Theatre Workshop and Joint Stock challenged the ideal of the star actor, but by the end of the century collaborative experimentation had become more orthodox than the systems it replaced.The second half of the book combines a helpful survey of the variety of realisms and alternatives to it on British stages with a more polemical argument for the gradual decline in the importance of writers in the theater. This decline was bound up, Shepherd implies, with the difficulty traditional British plays have expressing “desire, passion, and sexuality” (113). Shepherd would have us divide twentieth-century British theater makers into two camps, one more literary and one less so, named, oddly, after Roland Barthes’s distinction between two kinds of literary text, the “readable” and the “writable.” In the readable theatrical tradition, exemplified by Shaw, Travers, and Stoppard, irony and emotional reserve emerge as by-products of the prescriptive and authoritarian nature of the written text. In the writable tradition, Shepherd continues, plays gain the ability to express passion and to unsettle assumptions as they take on either more ambiguous or more distant relationships to authors. So while hints of the writable strain emerge in plays that encapsulate “the feeling of a historical moment” (143) (Terrence Rattigan’s The Deep Blue Sea [1952], John Osborne’s Look Back in Anger [1956]) or that unsettle realism’s certainties (Harold Pinter’s The Homecoming [1965], Caryl Churchill’s Fen [1983]), it is exemplified by forms less dependent on authors, including documentary theater; Artaudian spectacle; and atmospheric, physical, or devised theater. While overtly expressive plays and nontextual theater both deserve more attention than previous accounts have given them, it remains perplexing why Shepherd would yoke the two phenomena together. But despite its idiosyncratic argument, the third chapter contains several noteworthy sections, including a welcome overview of midcentury verse drama (129–34), a helpful analysis of subspecies of realism (136–57), an incisive summary of the ways documentary theater communicates the real without resembling it (158–64), and a diverse introduction to experimental and devised theater in the 1970s and ’80s (174–84). The final chapter argues that modern British theater should be remembered as much for its ideological movements as for its productions. While European aesthetic movements like naturalism, surrealism, and expressionism held relatively little sway in Britain, what mattered were political and social commitments. The chapter summarizes an admirable range of antiestablishment theatrical movements—feminist, gay, black, and disabled—but restricts its focus somewhat too often to the twenty years following 1970.Overall, the book offers a welcome break from chronology, but its piecemeal approach is likely to disorient students. Many sections offer excellent capsule histories, notably the discussion of repeated attempts to found a national theater (1–16) and the summary of alternative impulses since the 1960s (41–64). Nevertheless, a student would need to read bits of each chapter for a summary of British theater in the 1980s, for instance, and would have little guidance from the index in this endeavor. Fans of commercial theater and theater since the millennium will have even less luck. Although marketed as an introduction, the book assumes a reader already familiar with many of the major figures in modern theater. We are meant to recognize the closing lines of Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot despite no mention of its title (141), and no introductions prepare the reader for references to the likes of John Osborne, Joe Orton, Constantin Stanislavski, Jerzy Grotowski, Harold Pinter, or Caryl Churchill. Also disappointing is the narrowness of Shepherd’s definition of “British” to refer to theater written or performed in Britain by those who were born there. Those looking for an introduction to the contributions on London stages of prominent Irish-born authors—including seminal figures like Oscar Wilde, W. B. Yeats, and Samuel Beckett—might supplement this book with The Cambridge Companion to Twentieth-Century Irish Drama , edited by Shaun Richards (Cambridge University Press, 2004). Despite Shepherd’s emphasis on theater’s dispersal, there is no mention of British theater as it dispersed around the Commonwealth or as it was written in former colonies. If in these respects the book can feel all too British, some might find its conclusions not British enough. Shepherd’s tentative summation in the half-page afterword, perhaps better described as an afterthought, may prompt readers to wonder what is distinctly British about the book’s conclusions (228). After all, the cardinal developments he identifies—the emergence and potential decline of the director, the proliferation of new and nonmimetic acting and performance styles, the increasingly liminal position of authors, and the tension between commodification and experimentation—are arguably hallmarks of all Western theater since the late nineteenth century.
