title: Arthur Miller: Death of a Salesman/The Crucible. Readers’ Guide to Essential Criticism
abstract: In an ambitious and lucidly written critical study titled Arthur Miller: Death of a Salesman/The Crucible. Readers' Guide to Essential Criticism, Stephen Marino discusses in painstaking detail the biographical, critical, social, and cultural development of Miller's two most popular plays. Both Death of a Salesman and The Crucible have been recognized as the most often performed and most widely read plays in Miller's canon; indeed, Marino quotes Christopher Bigsby's assertion that the plays were written during the “Golden Age of American drama.”In the eight chapters that compose Marino's study, he carefully tracks the progressive development of the criticism that has accompanied the two works from the earliest reviews from 1949 to 1969 to the poststructuralist approaches that arose in the late 1980s and 1990s. Marino examines the early criticism that immediately followed the production of the plays in chapter 1, the elements of society and tragedy in chapter 2, the psychological and ethnic slants of the plays in chapter 3, the tenets of history, law, and politics in chapter 4, contemporary poststructural and feminist and gender readings in chapters 5 through 7, and finally media versions of the plays in chapter 8. Marino arbitrarily divides the critical response to the two plays into three periods: from 1944 to 1968, a “middle period” from 1968 to the mid-1980s, and a final era from the late 1980s to the present. He aptly discusses in detail the tension as well as the relationship between theater criticism and literary criticism as one considers the several facets of both plays. Marino states his purpose succinctly in his introduction: “This book aims to identify the seminal texts and major areas of discussion that have developed since Salesman and The Crucible premiered and highlight some of the major critics who have influenced the critical judgement of Miller's masterpieces.”The “Reviews and Early Criticism” highlighted in chapter 1 examine initial popular and scholarly reactions to Salesman and Crucible; while The Crucible received mixed reviews, some even negative and hostile, Salesman was heralded as an innovation in American drama. The “Early Criticism” section of the chapter reviews critical reactions to Willy Loman's “character”—his relationship to his society as well as that to his sons. Marino mentions the significance of the critical editions of Gerald Weales as catalysts that catapulted Salesman into the scholarly limelight. Marino continues in the chapter to discuss the dramatic form and style and the language of both plays and how these elements contributed to the positive scholarly response to the plays; then Marino continues by offering some examples of scholarly appraisals of how form, style, and language operate in the plays. The “Book-Length Studies” and “Comparative Studies” sections of the chapter offer examples of more divergent and more encompassing early reactions to the plays, with suggestions from some scholars that Miller's work could be compared to that of Tennessee Williams, Ibsen, and Shakespeare.Chapter 2, titled “1949-1979: Society and Tragedy,” reviews critical reactions to the two plays in the early years after their productions, and the chapter sustains the notion that both plays established Miller as a significant and emerging social dramatist whose characters and whose themes were singular examples of dramatic tragedy. Marino explains how Miller's pivotal essay “Tragedy and the Common Man” emerges as a central commentary on the “nature of the tragic hero in modern drama.” Marino then continues to explain and interpret the analyses of various scholars who view both Willy Loman and John Proctor as tragic heroes. The final section of the chapter explains the role of the American Dream ideology in the plays and offers various critics' notions of the presence in the plays of Americanism, the success myth, and the role of family.Chapters 3 and 4 examine various critical impressions of the two plays that arose in the 1980s, with chapter 3 discussing the notions of “Salesmanship, Psychology, and Ethnicity” in Salesman and chapter 4 examining the elements of “History, Law, and Politics” in The Crucible. Marino catalogues and records the reactions of several critics as they scrutinize these various components operating in the plays. The “Salesmanship” section in chapter 3 discusses the themes of business, profit, consumerism, and economics in Salesman. The “Psychology” section offers various hypotheses concerning Willy's isolation, his possible schizophrenia, his motivations and those of Biff, and the psychological tension that exists between the individual and society. The section titled “Characterization” presents a number of scholars' ideas about the significant nature of the characters, Ben, Linda, Hap, Howard, and Bernard, as well as examining the prevalent critical assessment of the Willy/Biff relationship. The “Ethnic Approaches” section examines how certain scholars discuss Miller's Jewish background as a motivating basis for Salesman while other critics view Willy as a more universal American prototype. Marino ends the chapter with Enoch Brater's assertion that Miller was able to transcend the Jewish influences in his upbringing when he wrote the play.Then Marino continues in chapter 4 with a study of the criticism of the 1980s with a thought-provoking investigation of various influences that produced The Crucible. Marino admits that, though early reactions to the play concentrated extensively on its connections to HUAC and McCarthyism, later critical assessments recognized that Miller was exploring a number of other relevant themes in the play, such as the “veneration for the law and the ritual of the trial” and the transformative power of guilt and suffering on the human psyche. Scholarly views of the play have progressed from initial political interpretations to more encompassing, psychological, spiritual, and moral observations.In chapter 5's discussion of “Tragedy, Dramatic Form, and Style” in Salesman, Marino notes the emergence of what he terms the “high” criticism of the 1990s that engendered scholarly debates concerning Willy's identity crisis, absurdism, and the mixture of realism and expressionism. In the “Salesmanship and American Dream” section, Marino examines the assertions of critics who concentrate on the changing plight of American business and the failure of capitalism and how these facets operate in the play. The “History, McCarthyism, and Tragedy” section illustrates continuing and innovative analyses of how The Crucible parallels the travails of the HUAC enigma as well as offering novel portraits of John Proctor as tragic hero and the concept of the “triangle tragedy” evident in the play. The “Character, Characterization, and Psychology” section examines a number of critical psychological approaches to Willy and Proctor in terms of, for example, the prevalence of Jungian concepts in The Crucible and the presence of shame and guilt in Salesman. The “Language” section explains how the 1990s brought a vacillation of interest in the actual dialogue and words in the two plays, with certain scholars noticing the recurrence of the concept and the word “weight” in The Crucible, the lyricism of the language in Salesman, and the “death-saturated dialogue” noticeable in the plays. Marino concludes chapter 5 by mentioning the 1995 founding of the Arthur Miller Society, whose formation served as a significant catalyst for the criticism that would follow into the twenty-first century.Chapter 6 continues studying the criticism of the 1990s by highlighting the feminism and gender studies that emerged in relation to the two plays. The feminist/gender studies of Salesman examined the inadequacies of the male business world, the weakness of the male characters, the faltering relationship that existed between Willy and his sons, and general comments that although the male presence seemed to be dominant in the play, the male psyche was consistently weak and unreliable. Other scholars viewed Linda as the typical 1940s housewife, while others saw her as the crucial sociological family element through which the men in the play define themselves. The feminist/gender approaches to The Crucible exhibited varying portraits of Abigail as female seductress, Elizabeth either as a “hag” or misunderstood wife, and Proctor as an individual who does not assume responsibility for his role in his adultery and who refuses to grasp how his actions have influenced the behavior of the women in the play. Marino mentions David Savran's study and its examination of the politics of masculinity operating in Salesman, The Misfits, and After the Fall.The critical trends that arose after 2000 are the focus of chapter 7. Marino divides the chapter into a number of sections in which he catalogues the various innovative reassessments of Salesman and The Crucible that materialized in the twenty-first century. The section on “Full-Length Studies” includes Christopher Bigsby's Arthur Miller: A Critical Study, Terry Otten's The Temptation of Innocence in the Dramas of Arthur Miller, and Jeffrey Mason's Stone Tower: The Political Theater of Arthur Miller. The “Collection of Essays” section presents some of the significant critical compilations such as those edited by Eric J. Sterling (which includes an essay by the late Steven R. Centola), the addition of two Miller texts by Harold Bloom to his Modern Critical Interpretation Series, and Brenda Murphy's editing of two collections—Arthur Miller in 2009 and Death of a Salesman in 2011. Marino in the “Biography” section asserts that Christopher Bigsby's two-volume biographies of Miller—Arthur Miller 1915–1962 and Arthur Miller 1962–2005—stand as the definitive biographies of the playwright. Finally, the “Essays” section highlights some of the individual essays that advance fresh analyses of the two plays by exploring props and staging, by noting previously unheeded flaws in Salesman, by examining the lack of realism in the plays, by presenting critical stances that question Proctor's heroism, and by establishing comparative connections between the two plays and other authors that scholars might tend to overlook.The final chapter offers a brief survey of film and television versions of Salesman and The Crucible from 1950 to 2000. A version of Salesman appeared as early as 1951, a CBS film, for American TV, offered a production in 1966 and again in 1985. Columbia Pictures' Career of a Salesman was produced to accompany the 1950 film adaptation, its purpose being to counteract the play's supposed depiction of the failure of American business. As would be expected, Miller strongly objected to Career. Marino mentions the renderings of Salesman with Lee J. Cobb and Dustin Hoffman, and he often references Brenda Murphy's comments on these adaptations for critical clarity. The Crucible has not fared as well as Salesman in media adaptations; Marino asserts that the plays of Tennessee Williams experienced more success on screen because Miller's plays were more rooted in the tenets of a live theater experience. However, some TV versions of The Crucible did arise, as well as the 1996 film version with Daniel Day-Lewis as Proctor. Interestingly, this chapter takes note of the 1957 French version written by Jean-Paul Sartre and titled Les Sorcieres de Salem, a version that concentrated on the play's adultery and emphasized the Marxist elements in the work. Both Christopher Bigsby and Miller offered strong objections to Sartre's screenplay.Marino concludes with an explanation of Miller's ever-increasing popularity both in the United States and especially in Britain. Both plays have become integral components of the literary curriculum in high schools, colleges, and universities. Just as this study highlights the opinions and stances of a number of scholars addressing the various themes in Death of a Salesman and The Crucible, so will future scholarship discover innovative modes of appreciating the two plays. Marino's book serves not only as a guide to and brief anthology of the ideas of various critics concerning relevant Miller themes, but also as a call to future scholars to continue the critical assessment of Miller's works. As Marino states in his final chapter: “The future publication of Miller's diaries, letters, notes and journals has the potential to redefine Miller criticism.” Marino's well-documented study has paved the way for such continuing criticism.

title: “Phil” (1969) by Chuck Close (b. 1940)
abstract: MICHAEL SALCMANserved as chairman of neurosurgery at the University of Maryland and president of the Contemporary Museum in Baltimore. As art critic and neuroscientist he writes and lectures on art and the brain; see him on The Knowledge Network of The New York Times. As a poet his work appears widely: Alaska uarterly Review, Harvard Review, Hopkins Review, New Letters, Ontario Review, Raritan, and New York Quarterly; collections include The Clock Made of Confetti (Orchises, 2007), nominated for The Poets1 Prize and a finalist for The Towson University Prize in Literature, and The Enemy of Good Is Better (Orchises, 2011).The human face is the most expressive mechanism for meta-communication in our environment; we read the face for recognition and understanding, in joy and sadness, in the home and in the theater stall. That which is said or thought is not believed unless the speaker's face registers a congruent emotion. We decorate our faces to emphasize fierceness in war and attractiveness in love. By analyzing subtle structural similarities in familiar faces, we recognize children and grand children and certify membership in our kinship or tribe. Little wonder that the artistic portrayal of faces is one of the oldest forms of art making. From ancient Greece and China to the Renaissance in Italy and down to the present day, portraiture has been a sub-genre of painting and sculpture. Portraits of rulers and gods in stone, metal, plaster and crystal in ancient Egypt were highly stylized profiles; unique personality and facial features first appeared during the reign of Akhenaten in the 14th century BCE. The 3300-year-old painted limestone Bust of Nefertiti (c. 1345 BCE) in Berlin's Neues Museum is one of the most famous examples. From ancient Greece, similarly realistic sculpted heads and coins of leading rulers and personalities survive, including representations of Alexander the Great and Socrates. According to literary evidence, the lost paintings of Greece possessed a similar verisimilitude. The Chinese portrait tradition goes back at least a thousand years BCE but the oldest surviving paintings, such as the Court Portrait of Emperor Shenzong of Song (c. 1067-1085, National Palace Museum, Taipei) come from about 1000 CE. Many Roman portrait busts survive but paintings from that period are rare, except for a few frescos and the marvelous full-face portraits used as funeral panels in the Fayum district of Egypt (2nd to 4th century CE). The first major decline in accurate portraiture occurred during the Middle Ages when realistic likenesses of religious donors and rulers became relatively uncommon. Notable exceptions include the early self-portrait by history's first great composer, the mystic polymath Hildegard of Bingen (1152) and the secular portrait of Charles IV by Master Theodoric in Prague (c. 1360-1380). The great turning point in the history of the portrait occurred during the Renaissance, both in Italy and in the North, when artists rediscovered the art of ancient cultures and attention turned to secular, humanistic subjects such as the human body. Change in philosophic and societal norms was accompanied by a variety of technical advances including anatomical dissection, the perfection of single-point perspective and the invention of oil-based paint. Willem de Kooning, the American Abstract Expressionist, famously said that oil paint was invented for the depiction of flesh. In fact, the reputed inventor of oil painting, Jan van Eyck (c. 1395-1445), was himself a great portraitist. Van Eyck's pioneering work was deepened and enlarged by virtually every important artist who followed him: in the North by Cranach, Durer and Holbein, in the South by Leonardo, Raphael and Titian. For the first time it was possible to form some estimate of the character of a person by studying their portrait. The world's most famous painting, Leonardo's Mona Lisa, is a portrait, Las Meninas by Velázquez is a group portrait and fully 10% of Rembrandt's paintings are self-portraits. From the Baroque and Rococo (van Dyck, Rubens, Velázquez), to English and American painters of the 18th century (Gainsborough, Reynolds, Copley, Stuart), and the Neo-Classical, Romantic and Realist artists of the 19th century (David, Ingres, Goya, Delacroix, Courbet) portraiture has thrived. The Philadelphian Thomas Eakins ranks among the greatest portrait artists since Rembrandt; surgeons and scientists are the subjects of many of his finest works.1 John Singer Sargent and Whistler were also exceptional portrait painters. Among the French Impressionists and Post-Impressionists, Manet, Renoir, Degas and Cézanne were expert and enthusiastic portraitists, often picturing one another. Vincent van Gogh, a sensitive Dutchman like Rembrandt before him, similarly devoted 10% of his paintings to self-portraits documenting every stage of his life. Although the development of photography in the early 19th century sharply reduced the need for painted likenesses, both Eakins and Degas were enthusiastic about the new medium and used it to help shape and inform their paintings. In the 20th century, photography freed painting from a strictly reproductive function and important painted portraits incorporated distortions of color and structure for emotional or philosophical purposes. This was true of the Fauves (Matisse, Derain), the Cubists (Picasso, Gris), the German Expressionists (Otto Dix, Max Beckmann) and the artists who moved in Dada or Surrealist circles (Miró, Max Ernst and Picabia). With the rise of Abstract Expressionism in the 1940s, portraiture by major artists dropped off for the first time since the Middle Ages. Their art and that of the Minimalists was so anti-realist that no portraits were thought possible. In the 1960s, only the Pop artists, primarily Andy Warhol and Jim Dine, created a substantial number of drawings and paintings devoted to the human face. The few artists who continued to paint recognizable portraits, like the realists Alice Neal, Fairfield Porter, Alex Katz and Philip Pearlstein, were considered “old fashioned” and marginalized by critics and art historians. Despite the work of Francis Bacon and Lucien Freud in London, it did not seem that a type of contemporary portraiture could be built on the same conceptual principles as Minimalism and Post-Minimalism.CHUCK CLOSE, b. 1940, Phil, 1969.Synthetic polymer on canvas, 108 1/4 x 84 x 2 3/4in. (275 × 213.4 × 7 cm). Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; purchase, with funds from Mrs. Robert M. Benjamin 69.102. © Chuck Close, courtesy The Pace Gallery. Photo by: Ellen Page Wilson/Courtesy The Pace Gallery.Into this void stepped Chuck Close (b. 1940), a member of the most distinguished graduate class in the history of any American art school. Charles Thomas Close was born in Monroe Washington and studied at the University of Washington in Seattle (1962) before obtaining his M.F.A. at Yale (1964). His friends in New Haven included 2 of the most significant Minimalist painters, Robert Mangold and Brice Marden, and a classmate, Richard Serra, arguably the most important Post-Minimalist sculptor. Surrounded by budding conceptualists and minimalists, Close was known for his brushwork and described himself at that time as a “junior” abstract expressionist. In 1966 he abandoned expressionism and started painting from photographs. Given his educational background the decision to become a portrait painter must have seemed perverse. After living in Europe and teaching in Massachusetts, he made the choice, in 1967, to make things even harder for himself by renouncing his facility with the paintbrush and forcing an artistic breakthrough. As Close later said, “I threw away my tools, I chose to do things I had no facility with. The choice not to do something is in a funny way more positive than the choice to do something. If you impose a limit to not do something you've done before, it will push you to where you've never gone before.”2 At first, Close was considered a conventional photo-realist and his work was linked to that of painters like Richard Estes or Audrey Flack, artists who projected photographs onto the canvas and who, with meticulous technique, turned their paintings into believable simulacra of the original transparencies. The comparison of his work with theirs was easily made but facile and superficial. Close did not project slides but used a modular grid, did not use color but painted in black and white, did not use brushes but a spray gun and, in order to counter the machine-like impersonality of the process, restricted himself to monumental portraits. The subject matter of the other “photo-realists” was almost always limited to inanimate objects: shiny cosmetic cases on a vanity (Audrey Flack), automobiles (Ralph Goings), reflective storefronts (Richard Estes), pinball machines (Charles Bell) and street signs (Robert Cottingham). Moreover, Close, in giving up his paintbrushes and thick luxurious paint, became a serious photographer who preferred shooting his friends with a large-format camera and black and white film. In recent years he has even started making Daguerreotypes. Close began his first paintings by tightly gridding a normal-sized photograph he had taken and then gridding a similarly sectioned (enormous) canvas in a ratio of 1 to 10. By graphing the photo and the canvas in strict proportion to one another he was ready to transfer all of the information contained in the photographic image to the ¼” squares of the painting. In this laborious cellular method, Close did not project his photograph on the canvas. The process was so accurate that he could tape off all of the adjacent cells on the canvas and do one at a time; it would still come out perfectly. The canvas might contain 1000 squares but Close would need only a few drops of paint and several months to create the transfer. Each cell within the grid received a spray of paint in a single average tonal value (ie, from black or very dark through grays or whites) that matched the one found in the corresponding cell of the gridded photograph. The technique echoed the dot screen matrix used by industrial printers to achieve tonal variations. Further manipulations of the paint by airbrush, rags, a razor blade, and an eraser mounted on a power drill were carried out until a perfect match was achieved. His first picture using this method was Big Self-Portrait (1968, Walker Art Center), 107.5 inches tall and 83.5 inches wide; it took him over 4 months to make and it is one of the least ingratiating self-portraits in the history of art. The 9-foot tall head of Chuck Close stares out at us through giant glasses, uncombed and unshaved, a cigarette drooping from the corner of his mouth, every pore and imperfection of his face intensely magnified. Thereafter, the inexpressive faces of his friends and himself, warts and all, blown up to gargantuan size, always seen from dead ahead (no profiles allowed) would comprise the sole subjects of his art! Within that narrow frame, Close has carried out an extraordinary exploration. Close had discovered an almost purely mechanical or machine-like way of creating a portrait. Except for the identity of his sitter, virtually every subsequent artistic decision was predetermined: the image taken from a gridded photograph, the modular method of applying the paint with an airbrush, the lack of color (en grisaille), the size and shape of the canvas (9-by-7 feet, vertical), the head, face and shoulders as sole subject, and the orientation of the sitter (face forward) were all part of a standardized process. Individual brushstrokes, ie, autographic evidence of the artist's hand, could not be seen and the surface of the painting was as flat as the surface of the source photograph. The use of arbitrary and repetitive rules completely divorced Close from the preceding generation of Abstract Expressionists and aligned him with the conceptual and minimal artists of his own time. Indeed, his mechanical way of working with the grid, a repetitive and identical form like the cube, recalls one of the fundamental organizing principles of Minimalism. As I have discussed elsewhere, the grid has been used as a tool to transfer pictures from small drawings to large surfaces since Renaissance times but only in the modern period did the grid itself become the subject of a painting or the shape of an object.3 Sol LeWitt's cellular structures and early drawings consisted entirely of 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional grids.4 Given the mathematical organizing principles of geometric shape and repetition, Judd's objects and LeWitt's structures could be fabricated from simple drawings or even written instructions supplied by the artist to workmen in a distant factory; the artist's hand was not necessary for realization of the object. For this reason, Conceptual art became a natural outgrowth of Minimalism and LeWitt famous for saying “the idea becomes a machine that makes the art.” For Close, the grid is both the painting's plan and the method by which he transfers spots of paint to the canvas, the artist working almost like an ink-jet printer, not to directly enlarge the image but to imitate the source photograph. In his first black and white paintings Close obscured the presence of the underlying grid; as his art matured, the grid became physically evident in the painted image. Given his mechanical way of working and the absence of visible brushstrokes, the early paintings of Close could, in theory, have been made by sending a photograph to a printer who would lithograph or silkscreen the image onto the canvas; in point of fact, the paintings derive some of their considerable power from our knowledge that a machine did not make these large, immaculate objects. Direct confrontation with impassive human faces larger than our bodies creates tremendous psychological impact; Close uses the size and scale of Minimalism to make the paintings rise up like ancient monoliths. title: The Four Poplars on the Bank of the Epte (1891) by Claude Monet (1840–1926)
abstract: When does Modern Art begin? There's no simple answer. Historians who take the long view might look to the Italian Renaissance and the discovery of single-point perspective, proper proportion and correct anatomical detail. Or consider the year 1800, when a preternatural foreshadowing of our present age can be discerned in the severely objective vision of David and the proto-surrealism of Blake and Goya. Social historians look to the rise of the modern city, urbanism, the isolation of the individual, and industrialization as hallmarks of the Modern Age. For these reasons, among many others, art historians and theoreticians believe that Edouard Manet was the first modern artist and 1863 the critical year when he sent for exhibition the Dejeuner and the Olympia to the Salon, those two marvelous paintings bristling with psychological implication for the viewer and the first attempt in the West, by way of the Japanese woodcut, to flatten Renaissance perspective. But the public cares little for such theoretical discourse and almost everyone today knows that Impressionism was the first organized art movement of the modern era and that Claude Monet was its leading artist. Indeed, even Manet, the pater familias of the French Impressionists, was heavily influenced by his young friends in the last phase of his career. In the Post-Impressionist generation that followed, Paul Cezanne liked to say that Monet “was only an eye, but what an eye” as if his stylistic predecessor had never used his brain. As we shall see, Monet's intuition served him well and he lived long enough to make a number of important contributions to modern and contemporary art. Today, when any exhibition of Impressionist masters brings in throngs of viewers, and the paintings bring many millions of dollars at auction, it is difficult to remember how reviled Monet was during much of his lifetime, harder still to accept the truly revolutionary nature of his work. But Monet's stature in art history compares favorably with his popularity. In his emphasis on the impression, the stroke, the contrast of colors, and the consistency with which he was often the first to make an advance, and to take it to its most logical and radical conclusion, Monet was truly “the exemplary Impressionist.”1 Claude Monet was born in Paris on the 14th of November, 1840; he showed no interest in inheriting his father's wholesale grocery store, drew caricatures of his classmates and by the age of 15 was receiving commissions for paintings. It was in 1856 that he met Eugene Boudin in Le Havre, a painter obsessed by the notion of painting outdoors (en plein air); in his maturity, Monet systematized this interest and painted the same subject over and over in all varieties of weather and lighting conditions. In this way, the magnificent series of Haystacks, Poplars, Rouen Cathedrals, Houses of Parliament, and Water Lilies were born. Based on recent developments in color theory, Monet and his friends became interested in an accurate, objective and scientific depiction of the atmosphere or light through which objects were seen at different times of day and at different seasons. Monet was one of the first artists in history to take such an approach and his serial investigation of a fixed form under varying conditions became a central tenet of modern art; his example influenced Cezanne's still life compositions and views of Mont St. Victoire, the still lives of Picasso and Braque, the abstract Homages to the Square by Josef Albers, the Black Paintings and Protractors of Frank Stella, and the Incomplete Cubes of Sol LeWitt. It is interesting to note that Monet's experiments in serial images began after the 8th and final Impressionist group exhibition in 1886, a time when the movement seemed to have come to an end, the group dispersed and Monet was criticized by Degas as a mere decorator.2 As a colorist, Monet employed a broken brushstroke technique in which small patches of intense color were placed side-by-side (without mixing) in order to pump up the chromatic impact of his compositions. He usually chose colors that were complements on the color wheel (eg, red/green, yellow/violet, blue/orange) and used them at a pitch that would cause visual vibrations. His “objective” or scientific study of his subjects often gave way to his interest in color (Impressionism) and the palette of reds, greens, blues and violets that he favored. His color sense influenced Gauguin, van Gogh and Matisse. Monet never stopped experimenting and lived long enough into the 20th century that he began to worry about becoming an old fogey, an artist who had been superseded by the Fauvism of Matisse and the Cubism of Picasso and Braque. So, while his corneal opacities worsened, Monet began to artificially sculpt the waters and gardens on his property in Giverny and allowed his canvases to become environmental in size and impact. Into these wall-size paintings, Monet inserted diaphanous and indistinct brushstrokes that almost completely vaporized the Water Lilies and their reflections. When the paintings of the 1920s were first installed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, their intense color, vigorous abstraction and landscape orientation greatly influenced the development of Abstract Expressionism. In this way, Monet achieved a sort of revenge on Cezanne and his immediate Modernist successors; Pollock and his colleagues would eventually destroy the abstract grid upon which Cubism was based. But the Poplar series, made by Monet in the Summer and Fall of 1891, contains within it the germ of the grid, that indispensible organizing principle of 20th century abstract art: the Cubism of Picasso and Braque, the Platonic world of Mondrian, the idealized Squares of Albers, the serial boxes of Judd and LeWitt. Of course, artists since the Renaissance have used the grid to “square-up” and transfer drawings to walls but only in the 20th century did the grid become the chief organizing principle and subject of paintings and sculptures. Although Monet would return to an implied grid in the etherealized façade of his later Rouen Cathedrals, paintings in which he employed a vertical plane to explore a vertical subject, the grid is most forcibly evident in the Poplars. Monet found his Poplar trees in a marsh along the banks of the Epte River, a few miles upstream from his home in Giverny where he created his famous gardens. The artist reached his floating studio, moored in the water, by a small boat in a nearby waterway; the trees were lined up in single file along the S-curve of the main part of the stream. He created 3 groups of paintings in all: in one, the towering poplars go off the top edge of the canvas, an effect seen in the present example from the Metropolitan Museum in New York. In another group, somewhat crowded, there are 7 trees and in the third, there are 3 or 4 trees without the severe cropping and en face orientation seen in the painting on our cover. The poplar series is the culmination of an 8-month period of study. At a certain point, Monet had to buy the rights to the trees because he had not finished painting them and could not risk having them cut down! When he was done he released the rights to a lumber merchant. In my opinion, The Four Poplars on the Bank of the Epte is the supreme achievement in the series. The 4 trees emerge from the riverbank with much of their foliage shorn or not yet in place; each trunk is perfectly replicated by its reflection in the river and each is placed equidistant from its neighbors. Indeed, the series of trunks begins and ends with the same amount of space from the right and left hand margins of an almost perfectly square canvas (32 1/4 × 32 1/8″). The 4 trees, the 4 reflections, the 5 columns of sky and water, and the horizontal riverbank, form an abstract grid. The tan and ochre trunks, the green leaves, and the riverbank grasses, are lit by a subtle sunset of reds and yellows, blues and pinks, their symmetrical reflections thrown into the water below. The rigidity of the grid is emphasized by the arbitrary amputation of the trees at the top of the canvas and the abbreviation of the reflections at its bottom. The presence of the grid in a typical Monet is made even more striking by his characteristic avoidance of outline and contour, his dissolution of line.1 Furthermore, unlike almost all the other paintings in the Poplar series, the trees are seen en face and not on a diagonal or from the side. This confrontational orientation, the flat grid-like presentation of the subject, not to mention the beautiful harmony of the colors, must account for the painting's powerful effect on the viewer and his visual system. Almost seventy years after Monet painted this scene, the symmetrical grid was ensconced in contemporary art and discovered to be one of the most efficient stimuli in eliciting cellular responses in the primary visual cortex of mammals. Before then, in one of the most beautifully titled and imaginative papers in the history of neurobiology, Jerry Lettvin and his colleagues at MIT demonstrated the excitatory response elicited by curvilinear shapes introduced into the receptive field of frog visual neurons3; the investigators hypothesized that such cells would act as “bug” detectors, allowing the frog to flick out its tongue at targeted prey. Based on this work, as well as Mountcastle's pioneering topographic studies of cellular responses in somatosensory cortex, Hubel and Wiesel began a series of experiments in the visual cortex of cats and spider monkeys that would win them the Nobel Prize.4 Sometimes “noise” boards with various rectilinear shapes, somewhat resembling late Kandinsky paintings or work by Franz Kline, were used to determine the general preferences of single cells in the retina, optic tract, lateral geniculate body and primary visual cortex of paralyzed animals facing a projection screen. Light bars of various orientations, from complete vertical to complete horizontal, were used to sharpen the preference of the cell and determine the size of its receptive field. Inputs of several of these “simple” cells were hypothesized to converge on a single “complex” or “hyper-complex” cell with the same orientation preference but larger receptive fields and a different pattern of surround inhibition and excitation.4 Some of the simple and complex cells were powerfully stimulated not just by a single bar moving across their receptive field but by a properly oriented grid of bars with a specific angular frequency, ie, a sine-wave grating similar to that seen in Monet's painting. Subsequent experiments in primates demonstrated the existence of multiple visual systems for shape, movement, and color, not to mention objects, numbers and faces, many of which systems would be optimally stimulated by the heightened properties of shape and color in a Monet painting such as The Four Poplars.5 Individual neurons in the visual system, as elsewhere in the brain, signal their excitation by a frequency code. In the case of stimuli with properties of angular or spatial frequency (ie, grids) or sounds with a particular auditory frequency (ie, pitch), the firing of neurons can directly reflect the spatial or temporal frequency of the stimulus.6 In fact, some mathematical treatments of neuronal output as a function of time (eg, an interspike interval histogram or ISIH) quite closely resemble the shape of the stimulus; the frequency of the peaks in the ISIH of a simple cell in area 17 of the monkey increases as the spatial frequency of a stimulating grid of light bars on the retina increases.7 Presumably this is just as true for a grid of poplar trees. The supposed simplification of art objects in the 20th century actually represents an intensification and isolation of the various component strategies that artists employ to excite the brain. Zeki has argued that artists are intuitive masters of neuropsychology. Calder's mobiles, the giant portraits of Chuck Close, the intense colors of Matisse and the spatial grids of Mondrian, Agnes Martin and Sol LeWitt all serve to maximally excite different visual pathways. In some respects, the progressive disentanglement of our many visual systems began with the beautiful colors and subtle insinuation of a modernist grid in The Four Poplars. Contra Cezanne, Monet was much more than a magnificent eye; he was a true revolutionary. The first of the impressionist painters to achieve success and the last to die, 40 years after his movement officially ended, Monet kept pushing his art decisively forward. Michael Salcman, MD Baltimore, Maryland

title: Arthur Miller's Century: Essays Celebrating the 100th Birthday of America's Great Playwright
abstract: As Stephen Marino rightly observes in his introduction to Arthur Miller's Century: Essays Celebrating the 100th Birthday of America's Great Playwright, this rich anthology of essays explores Miller's work from a wide range of approaches—“biographical, historical, political, comparative, language, psychology, feminist, cognitive, and dramatic theory and stagecraft” (xvii). The collection offers broad perceptions spanning the scope of Miller's texts and interesting insights into works not often treated. The brief abstracts following confirm the accuracy of Marino's assessment. Virtually all the contributions bear witness to Enoch Brater's claim in the foreword that “[e]ven after more than half a century [Miller's] voice rings true with alarming clarity” (xi).The anthology begins with two well-argued pieces, one extending across Miller's entire canon and the other focused on two earlier texts. The first chapter is a reprint of Christopher Bigsby's keynote address at the Arthur Miller Centennial Conference in 2015, titled “Performance and Arthur Miller.” The most eminent of Miller scholars, Bigsby applies his thesis to the whole of Miller's career and perceptively examines the sometimes ironic and ambivalent nature of “performance” that underlies the social and political realm and the private self. He argues that although “Miller's theatre was not polemical except at the very beginning when … he wrote plays for the trade union movement … he did write plays that staged the private consequences of private actions” (16), performance being an elemental human trait both onstage and off.Whereas Bigsby's contribution covers the whole sweep of Miller's work, Brenda Murphy's following essay centers on his seldom-discussed early attempt to write war journalism, Situation Normal. She explains Miller's growing anxiety when he unsuccessfully worked on a screenplay for producer Lester Cowan based on Ernie Pyle's Here Is Your War and discovered that the soldiers he tried to understand possessed a “personal faith in love for each other” that was “a far more potent factor … than any abstract belief” (22). Murphy explains Miller's epiphany as it is later reflected in All My Sons. As she concludes, the play “is in some sense the artistic outgrowth of the internal conflict that Miller records in Situation Normal … a play in which human relations have trumped ideological belief” (26).After these two persuasive studies, sixteen varied essays complete this major contribution to understanding the nature and significance of Miller's work. George Monteiro's “Gold, Football, and Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman” contends that a primary source for the play was the story of a legendary football coach at the University of Michigan, Gustave “Dutch” Ferbert, who after two highly successful years abandoned the university to join in the Alaskan gold rush, vowing to return only after making it rich. Ten years later, he did just that and came back with a million dollars in hand. Monteiro claims “that ‘Dutch’ and his story was the inspiration behind Miller's creation of Ben” (31) and that his tale was a shaping resource for much of the play.Citing reader-response theory's challenge to the idea of “a universal response to a given play or work,” Ramon Espejo Romero proposes reading “the unexplored global dramas of Arthur Miller's work” (37). His essay, “From ‘Universal’ to ‘Global’ Miller: Re-Writing the History of American Drama (Historian at Work),” recounts the history of drama in Spain leading to the repressive period of Francoism when Death of a Salesman was ironically the first major American play staged after the Madrid agreements in 1953. The Franco regime allowed the performance to deny that “Francoism was in fear of foreign culture” (42); however, despite the effort to interpret the play on the regime's terms, it transformed Spanish theater even though the play is so seemingly different from the Catholic culture of the country. Romero contends that it was “a Trojan horse” that shattered Francoist culture (40). He shows how Salesman, as well as The Crucible and After the Fall, introduced a “global perspective” that expanded “the limits of theater and literary studies” generally and “the Spanish theatre aesthetic” in particular (49).Brian Mazeski's contribution, “The Salesman at Sea: Aquatic Imagery in Death of a Salesman,” reflects the growing analysis of Miller criticism in response to the often expressed complaints of the dramatist's supposedly unsophisticated and unpoetic use of language. Building on earlier defenders of Miller's language, including Matthew Roudané, Stephen Marino, and Will Smith, he convincingly analyzes the aquatic imagery in the play to illustrate “Miller's unique dramatic idiom” (87).Matt Lorenz's “‘The Lightning of My Being’: The Byronic Struggle and Apotheosis of John Proctor” discusses how Proctor in The Crucible possesses many traits of the Byronic hero. Because of Byron's identity as essentially a poet of verse romances and poems, he may “seem to have more in common with the aspirations of novelists than of dramatists” and so “seems an unlikely influence on a twentieth-century American like Miller” (71). In fact, Lorenz contends, the Byronic hero parallels much “of the flawed nature of Miller's complicated heroes” (71).Richard Brucher's “Pragmatism and the Common Man” (a play on Miller's “Tragedy and the Common Man”) explores how the Arthur Miller associated with American Stalinists in the forties evolved by the early fifties into “a notorious anti-anti-Communist, a type of knee-jerk liberal” directly opposed by the recognized philosopher of pragmatism Sidney Hook and his followers. To Brucher, however, Miller's plays, and especially A View From the Bridge, reveal how pragmatism underlies the tragic dimension of his work. Centering on View, he characterizes Eddie Carbone's “pragmatic choices” and “defiance of agonizing, pragmatic choices” (80). In sum, Miller's dramas “help us know … how to anticipate unexpected consequences of our acts, especially if we believe that practical actions are necessary tests of our thoughts” (82). Garin Cycholl also addresses A View From the Bridge in “That World Fallen to Stones,” noting the similarities between Saul Bellow's Augie March and Eddie Carbone as characters caught between two worlds, a mythical old order and the new one “where everything has a price tag” (87). Comparing and contrasting the one- and two-act versions of the text, Cycholl describes Eddie's conflicted loyalties to the mythic old world represented by “the docks” and the need to cross over the boundaries into an emerging order. In his view, the docks appear “as a village” and provide the setting “for a distinctly ‘American’ tragedy” (89).In what will prove a controversial piece, Stefani Koorey exposes Arthur Miller's blatant sexism in “Arthur Miller Unzipped.” Beginning with how Miller exploited his relationship with Marilyn Monroe to direct attention away from his appearance before the House Un-American Activities Committee, she traces how he also exploited female characters in his plays—“Miller fabricates his female characters to serve the dramas of his decidedly masculine protagonists…. Women in Miller's literature are primarily configured to substitute or divert attention from the male action” (95). Koorey's unqualified condemnation of Miller's “patriarchal literary world view” (96) presents a formidable challenge to those who wish to question her claim. Some critics have, of course, contested parts of her argument in reference to given works and female characters, but the breadth of the case against Miller's treatment of women both on the stage and off will likely provoke other lively debate. Not exactly “celebrating … America's great playwright,” her essay is the most controversial text in this highly provocative anthology.Sylvia Kasey Marks interestingly directs attention to Miller's stories that critics have pretty much ignored or analyzed for essentially autobiographical references. She finds echoes from Miller's dramas in the stories, especially those collected in I Don't Need You Any More, published in 1967. She primarily assesses three tales, “I Don't Need You Any More,” “Fitter's Night,” and Jane's Blanket, describing how they all mirror the plays and potentially provide “a gloss on all of Miller's work” (117). In another convincing comparative study, Paul J. Contino presents a probing analysis of the idea of nadryv in The Brothers Karamazov and The Price, “Nadryv in New York: Dostoevskian Lacerations in Arthur Miller's The Price.” Noting Miller's long admiration of The Brothers Karamazov (he first read it as a teenager and at one point plotted writing it as a screenplay that might conceivably allow Marilyn Monroe to play Grushenka), Contino highlights the striking similarities between Victor and Walter Franz and Zosima and Alyosha. Both works portray nadryv, he asserts, “the lacerating psycho-spiritual dynamic in which characters perversely enact by playing a false role of self-sacrifice, in order to gain power in the eyes of another” (120). The next essay addresses another seldom-examined text, The Creation of the World and Other Business. Frank Bergmann looks at “Archetype and the Rhythm of Decorum” in the infrequently staged play and draws the intriguing conclusion that Northrop Frye may well have been right in asserting that though the play is hardly Miller's “best goddamned play,” as the playwright once declared, “it may well be his most central” (133).Ann Hall's “‘The Times, They Are A-Changin’: Time and Politics in Arthur Miller's Broken Glass and Harold Pinter's Ashes to Ashes” is the last extensive comparative study in the collection. Hall argues with insightful readings that in confronting the Holocaust both dramatists employ time in a “non-realistic” way that dissolves the seeming distinction often drawn between Miller's so-called realistic vision and Pinter's association with the absurdists. Both employ “methods that not only dissolve the years between the historical event and the present, but also dissolve the traditional distinctions used to describe their works” (135). Her engaging readings of both texts invite others to contest the often simplistic attempts to label Miller's work. Both dramas, Hall asserts, depict the Holocaust “from an altruistic spatial and temporal vantage point” and “connect political and domestic violence” (141)—and both portray the leading female characters as agents of necessary change “in terms of past, present, and future” (143).The remaining contributors to the anthology are especially well-known Miller scholars. In “The Last Yankee: Tragedy and Two Kinds of Pride,” David Palmer, the current president of the Arthur Miller Society, answers why Miller called The Last Yankee “a comedy about a tragedy.” Palmer sees the text “as a portal toward understanding Miller's broader vision of tragedy,” especially “a peculiarly American tragedy” and how it “rises from a faulty sense of pride … grounded in the dark side of the American dream” (145). In his thorough exploration of the text, he reveals how the play resonates with other Miller texts in dramatizing how the sense of pride generated by the absurd notion of the American Dream translates “from authentic pride to hubristic pride” (158). This cogently argued essay resurrects long pursued questions about Miller's concept of tragedy in a culture that seemingly challenges its very nature.In one of the most impressive studies in this collection, Jane K. Dominik, past president of the Arthur Miller Society, provides an inventive and convincing treatment of absent characters in Miller's plays beginning with They Too Arise and extending to the end of his career. “Empty Chairs, Pools of Light: Absent Characters in Arthur Miller's Drama” surveys the broad range of “characters who never appear on stage in the present time” but “become central to characters' conflicts, motivations, and dilemmas” (162). Dominik illuminates the ways Miller employs “objects, lights, music, conjuring, unseen Listeners, or silent bodies” to project absent figures and shows how these various strategies move “his play away from so-called realistic drama to impressionism, abstract expressionism, symbolism, surrealism, absurdism, minimalism, and magical realism” (180). This penetrating and important study again opens doors to further critical analyses.The founding and current editor of The Arthur Miller Journal, Stephen Marino, dares to characterize Miller as “Brooklyn's Shakespeare.” His inventive reading investigates the “startling comparisons in their biographies” (185), not least of which how both artists lived in strikingly similar worlds. He compares the writers' histories, their families, their gradual introduction to theater, their subsequent need to leave family to pursue stage careers, their common struggles to tread “the treacherous political and religious waters of their times” (189), and, most significantly, their shared pursuit of tragedy. “Just as Shakespeare's plays defined Renaissance tragedy,” Marino concludes, “Miller's essay, ‘Tragedy and the Common Man’ re-defined tragedy for the modern era” (189). In short “Arthur Miller is Brooklyn's Shakespeare for the legacy he left” (189).Susan C. W. Abbotson, long associated with the Arthur Miller Society and Miller scholarship, also adds a highly rewarding biographical perspective in “Miller and Morath in Collaboration.” Beginning with the chilling history of Inge Morath's survival of World War II and her subsequent emergence as a world-class photographer whose ability “to view a person's inner nature and capture it through her lens” (194) mirrors Miller's portrayal of stage characters, Abbotson labels their union “a true marriage of equals” (194). Incorporating several powerful copies of Morath's photography, she characterizes her art and summarizes her first meeting Miller and their nearly forty years together. Despite having separate careers, she notes, Morath and Miller shared a common vision and effectively worked together on three different books. Exploring these works, Abbotson discovers many “excellent insights into Miller's beliefs, fears, and hopes” and leads to the undeniable conclusion that Morath and Miller's relationship and collaboration have been “for too long critically ignored, and appear eminently worthy of closer inspection” (214).The last entry in the volume appropriately reasserts what Bigsby's initial entry contends and other essays confirm, that Miller holds an enduring place in American drama. In “Arthur Miller: A Career of Commitment,” Joshua Polster, also a past president of the Arthur Miller Society, assesses Miller's continuous commitment “to the arts and humanities in order to advance social awareness, engagement and progress” (215). His summing up highlights key stages in Miller's biography, demonstrating again how the playwright stayed true to his convictions in his life and work and repeatedly expressed “his willingness to engage in difficult conversations and take on societal problems that needed to be addressed” (229). He speaks for all Miller admirers when he argues that onstage and off, Miller's presence is felt, that his “dramas and political activism continue to serve and powerfully resonate” (231).As these brief abstracts testify, Arthur Miller's Century not only succeeds in celebrating Miller's life and work, but also offers new or redefined strategies for further exploration in its variety of approaches and insights. A centennial is surely the proper time to pay tribute, but it is also the right time to reassess, revise, and redirect the body of criticism addressing an author's life, work, and place. The far-ranging perspectives expressed in this collection give deserved acknowledgment to early studies, but open new avenues of assessment and understanding as well.

title: Lasting Impressions: The Legacies of Impressionism in Contemporary Culture by Jesse Matz
abstract: There can be few movements in art to have suffered such dramatic reversals as Impressionism. Initially it shocked conservative tastes not just for the political radicalism of its focus on the seamier side of Parisian life and leisure—sexuality, prostitution, drink—where the bourgeoisie and lower classes got adulterated, but also for the way its programmatic immediacy and rapidity issued in works that to viewers accustomed to realism seemed like scandalously unfinished sketches. The movement famously got its name in 1874 when, during its first group show, the critic Louis Leroy scoffed at Monet’s “Impression: Sunrise,” titling his review in Le Charivari “The Exhibition of the Impressionists.” But the group liked the term, and adopted it. When young Henry James saw their second show in Paris two years later, he was comparably unimpressed: “To embrace [these artists] you must be provided with a plentiful absence of imagination. . . . The Impressionists . . . declare that a subject which has been crudely chosen shall be loosely treated. They send detail to the dogs and concentrate themselves on general expression” ([1876] 1956, 3). To James, Impressionism’s audacious provisionality seemed inimical to artistry. To Ruskin, in another defining moment of contemporary resistance to Impressionist aesthetics, it appeared a contemptuous confidence trick. Writing about Whistler’s “Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket,” exhibited at the Grosvenor Gallery, he said: “I have seen, and heard, much of Cockney impudence before now; but never expected to hear a coxcomb ask two hundred guineas for flinging a pot of paint in the public’s face” (1903–12). Whistler sued, and won the case. But the damages, notoriously set at a farthing, indicated that the judge sided with Ruskin, and the trial bankrupted Whistler.As waves of new, modernist movements broke in the early twentieth century—Fauvisme, Cubism, Die Brücke, Futurism, Vorticism— Impressionism was no longer avant-garde. By 1910, when Roger Fry curated the first post-Impressionist exhibition in London, Impressionism was something in relation to which you were supposed to be post-. Of course Impressionism didn’t just cease. One of the many virtues of Jesse Matz’s earlier book, Literary Impressionism and Modernist Aesthetics (2001), is its demonstration of Impressionism as an influence persisting through the modernism of writers such as Proust, the later James, Conrad, Ford, and Woolf.The avant-garde view that Impressionism had swiveled round from being a revolutionary provocation to a tedious convention reflected the converse volte-face in public taste. As Impressionism was acquired by museums and collectors, it became the standard of modern beauty, and so it has remained in the art world, or at least in the world of blockbuster exhibitions, museum merchandising, and art for investment. Impressionism continues to draw the biggest crowds, generate the most mechanical reproductions, and achieve the highest auction prices.It is this curious persistence of Impressionism—despite post-Impressionism, despite abstraction, despite conceptualism, despite postmodernism—that provides Matz with the central subject of his brilliant new book, Lasting Impressions. What does its persistence tell us about Impressionism? And what does it tell us about ourselves, and our subsequent aesthetics? Matz begins, engagingly, with a confessional reminiscence. He is fifteen. The two still lifes that hung in his childhood home, and which he had barely attended to, are described by a sophisticated friend as examples of “pseudo-impressionism,” and he sees them differently: as examples of “false artistry” and “fake luxury” (1). The rest of the book traces how these subthemes—of kitsch, on the one hand, and trickery, on the other—appear inseparable from the legacies of Impressionism. Researching the painter of those still lifes, the Hungarian émigré Béla Kontuly, Matz is surprised to find that he had been a modernist before the Second World War. For a Western modernist, a turn to Impressionism in the 1960s would seem a regression, an anachronism, a turning of his back on Abstract Expressionism, yet Matz argues that it could equally be read as an escape from an enforced Socialist Realism, a declaration of the freedom of individual perceptions and styles.This could be the introduction to a very fine book focused solely on the legacies of Impressionism in painting and—given Matz’s earlier book—in literature too. These certainly provide two central lines through Lasting Impressions, as we shall see. But the most striking thing about the book is how much more it offers. It also takes in music, advertising, cinema, tricksters, the art market, the mass marketing of reproductions, and, in a surprising but dazzling conclusion, books popularizing cognitive science and books about autism. Taken together, the case these explorations assemble so cogently is that notions of the “impression” remain central not only to our aesthetics but also to our philosophy of mind, our economy, and our social and political life. “Impressionism,” says Matz, “is everywhere” (18).The opening chapter explores “Histories for the Tache”: the signature Impressionist touch, spot, or brushstroke, and the “dual nature” it has repeatedly been understood as displaying—both the guarantee of the phenomenological reality of the rendered perception and a sign of the paintedness of the surface, the facticity of the artwork. If the technique “could simulate something real, it also expressed the artist’s individual personality” (37). In the second chapter, “The Impressionist Advertisement,” Matz explores another side of this technique. He begins with a hostile review from 1874, in which Jules-Antoine Castagnary argued that Cézanne offers a lurid warning revealing what happens to those who “pursue the impression to excess”: “Starting with idealization, they will arrive at that degree of unbridled romanticism where nature is merely a pretext for dreams and where the imagination becomes powerless to formulate anything but personal, subjective fantasies without any echo in general reason, because they are without control and without possible verification in reality” (quoted in Matz, 72). Matz argues that, according to this view, Impressionism ushers in the “shallow culture of meaningless sensation” (73) that Baudrillard was to deplore a century later: “It led, in other words, to advertising,” and “the main problem with advertising is its impressionism.” That is characteristically shrewd, though it needs setting against a far worse problem: that advertising, far from representing fantasy without control, attempts precisely to control our fantasies so as to achieve unconscious manipulation of our desires for commercial ends. In case studies of particular advertisements, though, Matz discovers a more nuanced dialectic. Those ads drawing on the avant-garde potential of inchoate perceptions have proved problematic, introducing a gap between image and text. In those drawing on the familiarity of Impressionism, then—Matz’s example here is the 1992 Levi’s campaign of “The Swimmer,” based on John Cheever’s story about a man pool-hopping his way home through the suburbs (but with Cézanne’s bathers also in the background)—what from one point of view is a kitsch banalization of a serious critique is in fact “a spur to serious pleasure and valid judgement . . . an ongoing project of perpetual aesthetic emergence” (98). This duality becomes the dominant theme of the second half of the book: it is precisely those productions likeliest to invite denigration as kitsch or con that prove sites of the most interesting “aesthetic emergence,” forging new forms and styles out of Impressionism’s bargain debasement.The third chapter, on French cinema, analyzes the influential notion of photogénie: a problematic term intended to convey the essence of cinema as art. Skillfully unpacking its ambiguities, Matz concludes that, ultimately, “photogénie is a fetishized version of the impression” (113); in other words, that while early theorists of cinema thought they were trying to analyze the new medium, they were also still working through the contradictions of Impressionism: its dual power to evoke reality and the phantasmatic. Lasting Impressions then takes a global turn, moving away from America and Europe to consider “The Image of Africa.” Matz gives an excellent analysis of Chinua Achebe’s rejection of Conrad’s work as racist, relating it to colonial literary education and to Achebe’s own fictional aesthetic; Africa, according to Achebe, is reduced in Heart of Darkness (1899) “to the role of props for the break-up of one petty European mind” (quoted in Matz, 133). To whatever degree one thinks Conrad is implying a critique of imperialism, “it is the height of corrupt imperialist fraud, this relocation of large-scale cultural trauma to the tragic ‘consciousness’ of those actually responsible for it” (133). What was required—and what Achebe’s own fiction provides—is a realism adequate to “Africa’s social context” (136). Things Fall Apart (1959) is “directly antithetical to Conrad’s impressionism because it reflects the power of African social life to overdetermine subjective reality rather than its incapacity to shape it.” The implication that Africa has a single “social context” might give us pause, especially in an argument about an imperialist reduction of the Congo to a crisis in Kurtz’s or Marlow’s subjectivity. In fact, this chapter attends with nuance to writers from, or writing about, several different countries—Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, Buchi Emecheta, and Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie—and to how the problem was just as much the educational system, which, however well-intentioned as a preparation for independence, nonetheless imposed the British canon.Matz then goes on to offer what seems like a counter-argument, central to his book, about realist writers following Achebe: “This antithetical tragic realism, however, retains a Conradian sense of the problem of the subjective impression. Conrad’s way of writing the image of Africa provoked a postimpressionist realism designed to make the impression’s duality more reliably one of self and world, Achebe’s work, and then the ‘School of Achebe’ that his realism inspired, developed a postimpressionist mode in which perceptions could emerge into political consciousness” (136). This is the characteristic turn that Lasting Impressions traces across the long twentieth century and its various media: the rejection of Impressionism entails a return to and rethinking of the impression, allowing new aesthetic configurations to emerge.Chapters 5 and 6 explore two grounds on which Impressionism has been rejected. “The Impressionist Fraud” juxtaposes three very different cases of figures attacked as tricksters: aesthetic showman Yves Klein, whose blue “monochromes” sought to engage with perceptual process in Impressionist ways, and James Frey, whose memoir of recovery from alcoholism, A Million Little Pieces (2003), endorsed by Oprah Winfrey, notoriously proved to be a work of fiction. In between these two, Matz discusses Ryoei Saito, the Japanese entrepreneur whose legendarily high bids for Impressionist works at auctions contributed to what was perceived as “the Japanese impressionism bubble” (185), and who was subsequently exposed as a financial fraudster with little care for art (he joked he would have Van Gogh’s portrait of Dr. Gachet cremated with him). If Impressionism from the start conjured anxieties about its sleight of hand, and associated commercial trickery (remember Ruskin contra Whistler), Matz sees these later tricksters as showing it as emerging into new forms of playfulness.Art fraud implies a conscious desire to hoodwink someone about the originality or value of an artwork. In chapter 6, on contemporary art, Matz attends to a case where belated Impressionism is berated as a form of kitsch—a species of unconscious fraud, in which the derivative work pandering to popular sentimentality passes itself off as original and worthwhile. Thomas Kinkade, as Matz puts it, “made his name at the shopping mall, peddling the imagery of nostalgia”: a world of folksy rural beauty, illuminated with a supernatural glow. Many malls have outlets for reproductions of his work, which, bizarrely, customers can pay to have customized with some taches added by the hand of a store employee. This seems the clearest-cut case imaginable of a debased and commercialized pseudo-impressionism. Matz contrasts Kinkade with a very different artist who nonetheless also evokes Impressionism’s visual style: Peter Doig, whose work doesn’t aspire to an Impressionist look but draws on its textures and motifs to produce work that is at once beautiful, referential, and innovative.Then, in another breathtakingly antithetical move, Matz writes that “Kinkade is not therefore a hopeless case. If his pseudo-impressionism is kitsch because it fails to make his kitsch aesthetic a subordinate part of a postconceptual art project, perhaps it only takes a postconceptual project to redeem his pseudo-impressionism—to make it too a proper form of art“ (222). This is more than an elegant speculative antithesis. He describes just such a project, “staged by Jeffrey Vallance, an installation artist associated with the ‘infiltration’ art movement,” who became “the first (and still only) curator to mount a show of Kinkade’s work”: Thomas Kinkade: Heaven on Earth (2004), at California State University, Fullerton. The show presented Kinkade’s oeuvre, and his world, as an art installation, thus foregrounding the very question kitsch discourages, of how to look at and understand the work of art. Vallance advocates a strategy of “dissonance arousal,” whereby the “cognitive dissonance” (quoted in Matz, 223) of such an experience—of being encouraged to look critically at kitsch in a museum setting—results in an effect of transcendence. People came expecting to hate the work but enjoyed the exhibition (Oh no, it’s kitsch! Wait, look, it’s meta-kitsch!). It is a further example of belated impressionism finding itself at the contemporary cutting edge.Chapter 7 on “The Pseudo-Impressionist Novel,” draws on David James’s work on the afterlife of Impressionism in contemporary fiction to juxtapose three novels with especially close relationships to Impressionist precursors: W. G. Sebald’s Austerlitz (2001), with its knowing reference to Proustian involuntary memory, and two novels that make impressionist authors central characters: Michael Cunningham’s The Hours (1998) and Colm Tóibín’s The Master (2004). Here Matz’s argumentative strategy comes home with full and disconcerting force. Each book is initially critiqued as succumbing to pseudo-Impressionist kitsch. The fact that the involuntary memories triggered in Austerlitz are of the Holocaust debases both the experience of the victims and the methods of impressionism. That Tóibín’s Henry James evades articulating his homoerotic desire even to himself seems to Matz a failure of impressionism to register the disturbances of mental life. Similarly, Cunningham’s aestheticization of Woolf’s suicide and modernization of the story of Mrs. Dalloway are seen as lacking the very qualities that make Woolf’s writing so existentially challenging.Then Matz crafts some cognitive dissonance of his own. Such Holocaust memories as are triggered in Austerlitz are enigmatic, uncanny traces of experiences not his in the first place. Rather than failures of impressionism, they are failed impressions put to ingenious, evocative, postimpressionist, and postmodern uses.
