title: Response to Fred Rush and Adrian Daub
abstract: I am very grateful to both commentators for the thoughtfulness of their questions about and for the generosity of their interpretations of After the Beautiful. I assume in the book the value of the category of artistic modernism. As I understand it, that means accepting the claim that, at some historical point in the development of ambitious fine art in the West, techniques, approaches, subject matters, and the embodiment of aesthetic norms, which had all been able to compel conviction successfully, to arrest attention, and to invite an appreciation that was distinctly aesthetic, not merely agreeable or entertaining, could less and less be counted on to achieve such results. This involved but went far beyond a growing indifference to the ideal of mimetic reproducibility or some sort of staleness in representational realism. Nothing now could be taken for granted about art itself; not its nature, its purpose, its importance, and so forth. In some way it seemed under a kind of threat or in some sort of crisis. I single out what I call “pictorial” modernism as a chief example and ask whether Hegel's historical approach to aesthetic meaning might be of use in understanding the issues. By that term in the subtitle, I did not mean to single out any continuing realist or representationalist or figural strain within modernism. The adjective was intended to announce that the treatment would not take in all visual art as such, not architecture, sculpture, photography, or film, and certainly not musical or literary modernism. The subject matter was easel painting; “pictures” in the sense in which Rothko and Pollock “painted pictures.” This of course raises the question of whether Hegel's approach in itself nevertheless still requires that we have to cut out too narrow a swath of pictorial modernism to understand the phenomenon. Fred Rush mentions a “Dionysian” strain within modernism, the effect of which is a liberation of subjectivity from normative constraints, something that does not seem included within the Hegelian picture. He also calls this a “musical” model of modernism.1 After all, I only discuss in any detail paintings by Manet and Cézanne. If the account is also relevant to movements like abstract expressionism, how would that go? And what about post‐60s art or the postmodern? Might not different, even early strains require a non‐Hegelian approach, and might not Hegel's fade in significance as the twentieth and twenty‐first centuries in art lurch and stumble forward? Such questions first turn on what it means to invoke “Hegel's approach” in understanding works that came after Hegel and especially after the greatest rupture in the tradition of pictorial art. There are two features of his approach that raise questions in both sets of comments. First, I argue that for Hegel art works involve a distinctive sensible–affective modality of intelligibility. Ultimately, in the full Hegelian picture in all its glory, this means a distinct way (in what one senses and feels) of rendering intelligible the Absolute, just as religion embodies a “representational” way (a kind of picture thinking) and philosophy a conceptual way. The Absolute for Hegel is “the Idea,” a notion that has many emanations: “the subject–object identity” is a familiar instance that Adrian Daub cites. I understand it to amount to full reflective self‐consciousness about the very possibility of intelligibility itself, practical as well as theoretical. That interpretation is, or has been, a controversial one in the last twenty‐five years, but it need not detain us here.2 It is at least the case that Hegel thinks of art as a distinct vehicle of collective self‐knowledge over historical time. What is crucial for Rush's concerns is the idea of a sensible–affective modality of intelligibility itself and what it has to presume about what he calls the “concept–percept” relation. He is right to note that this is the central and most difficult philosophical issue at stake. Hegel's theory of art, developed along these lines, does not invoke much of a notion of aesthetic experience or pleasure (and so he does not traffic much with the traditional idea of the beautiful) and embodies an approach in which a critical assessment of such distinctly artistic meaning is what is most called for, rather than an appreciative response guided by “taste.” (Or it involves the latter only as it is understood to be the former.) The second distinctive feature of a Hegelian approach involves the imbrication of questions about aesthetic meaning—especially given the assumption that all aesthetic meaning and significance are always historically indexed—in larger questions about socio‐political, cultural, religious, and philosophical developments, themselves always also requiring a historical diagnosis. This aspect raised several questions for both commentators. These could be classified as involving the Hegelian problem of “recognition” (and so ultimately potential reconciliation) and the usefulness of that term for understanding art and developments in art history. So, to begin, I would not say that my Hegel “will valorize realism” but rather valorizes, treats as the most significant issue, the problem of aesthetic intelligibility.3 This is what makes Hegel so useful for understanding these developments, because, at least as I read them, that is also what it is at issue in the paintings that became so controversial. What is important about Manet's Olympia and other modernist paintings understood this way is not so much (or not just) that what appears to be her puzzling, somewhat hostile form of address to whoever is in front of her within the tableaux embodies in that social exchange some sort of struggle for recognition, and one that is failing. Rather by often bringing his subjects much closer to the picture plane and by actually “de‐realizing” the mode of presentation, flattening the main subject, avoiding the sculptural modeling of figures that suggests solidity, violating the laws of vanishing point and aerial perspective, and leaving the painting in an apparently “unfinished” state, the painting's mode of address to the beholder is at issue, and the elements of painting just as painting (foregrounded by these techniques) are thereby in effect presented for consideration, and this in a challenging, quasi‐ironic “tone,” as if traditional answers about the nature and significance of ambitious painting are no longer available. Olympia's gaze is the sign that we are in uncharted waters. (I make use here of Michael Fried's account of the “facingness” at issue in the painting and in Manet and beyond.4) As Rush realizes, there is nothing about this that is wedded to figural representation. The key Hegelian element is the emphasis on the question of what is to be the presumed relation between the painting, or the work of art, and the beholder or listener or reader addressed, what is implied in the form of address, what is implied about the response expected. There are other elements in the modality of painterly intelligibility and in the assumed significance of attempts at painterly intelligibility that could be interrogated in this way: shape, pictorial organization, color, relations among colors, solidity and weight, paint itself, brushwork, thickness, different representational regimes thematized as such, expressive tonality, elements of line and boundary, and so on into the history of painting after Manet and Cézanne.5 (Daub ties the approach I take too closely to figural meaning. In the terms set out here, I do not see why the issue being explored by Picasso in “the eyes of the Desmoiselles d'Avignon” cannot be subject to just this sort of analysis.6) It is of course extremely controversial to suggest that visual intelligibility itself, in, and independent of, painting, can “have a history” in this way, especially in an era in which we think the issues are wholly those of cognitive neuroscience. But such is Hegel's position.7 It is in this context that I can address two of Rush's main concerns. The most concise form of his question is “how sight might be a form of conceptual life.” The “concept–percept” relation involved in that question is the most difficult to discuss economically. Perceiving, including aesthetic perception, as Hegel understands it, is not itself judging but must be a taking up of a sensory deliverance that itself must be of the form that makes it a suitable basis for a judgment. So perceptual experience itself could be said to be pre‐judgmental and in that sense pre‐reflective, but that does not mean it should be understood as devoid of conceptual content. It can be said to have conceptual content in potentia, determinately, and in this way to be conceptually articulated.8 Perceptual content must be the sort of content that can play the role it must in perceptual judgment and so must be conceptual in this sense.9 Rush suggests that the phenomenon of “looking” can be helpful in exfoliating the idea, but the point seems to me more general. In the book I suggested that Hegel's understanding of bodily movements, when rightly understood as actions, can be of some help as well in understanding how Hegel thinks that material objects and events can be said to bear meaning (or how material content can be conceptually informed, in a way different from the “imposition” of a concept on a material, or by virtue of a causal relation between a distinct mental intention and a bodily movement).10 That account does not permit any brief summary. The upshot is that the example is supposed to make clear, first, that Hegel is not intellectualizing aesthetic experience. The mode of aesthetic intelligibility or conceptuality is distinct: a sensible mode, not a judgmental or discursive mode. There is no “idea” clothed in sensible form. The idea is the idea it is only in such embodiment. Second, whatever mode is at issue, that mode must be sharable and can be contested. It is in this sense that the issue of “recognition” is relevant to Hegel's account of aesthetic intelligibility or, indeed, all intelligibility. (That is, the register at which it is relevant is not limited to the so‐called “content” of, say, Olympia. The painting's own intelligibility as a painting, for a beholder, depends on the issue.) Whatever assumption is presupposed about such sharability within a community at a time will also be reflected in the assumptions about a painting's address to the beholder and that beholder's presumed response. In any claim about what is the case or what ought to be done, a commitment is made and a certain form of answerablity is assumed. This is assumed to be relevant to a painting's implicit address to a beholder, and a beholder's presumed response. These conditions can change, can come under pressure, even a severe sort of pressure of a sort far more drastic than Hegel had imagined, and in a way that we should also expect to see at issue in various social transactions and claims to legitimacy. (Here I agree with Rush about the value of T. J. Clark's explorations of these issues and I try to say why in Chapter 3.11) Rush also raises difficult questions about the attempt to separate Hegel's “teleology” from his “dialectic” and about “reconciliation.” Normally, when one hears that former issue being raised, especially in the left Hegelian tradition, the idea is that one can isolate dialectic as a method and divorce oneself from Hegel's triumphalist claims about historical progress. I have not attempted such a radical separation and suggest in the concluding chapter that there are aspects of Hegel's “teleological” account of historical development that are worth preserving and that are essential to a potential Hegelian understanding of modernist art. In the account defended there “teleology” and “dialectic” are inseparable in Hegel. The key is to understand such a teleology in practical rather than theodocical or theological terms. Briefly, that would involve the claim that a significant transition in art history or political history or religious history, a shift in collective ethical commitments, can be rendered intelligible by a philosophical account on the assumption of some purposive group agency. This account is based on a form of practical contradiction (and “progress” in overcoming it) that introduces a more familiar form of teleological necessity, the form appropriate to “he who wills the end must will, or necessarily wills, the means” (otherwise we have evidence that he has not willed the end). If a collective attempt to accomplish some goal can be said to learn collectively that commitment to that end is impossible without commitment to, let us say, a broader and more comprehensive end, then it must pursue such a new end or give up the enterprise. Or, if it develops that the means chosen actually make achieving the end impossible, then the means must be altered. They are not arbitrarily altered. They must be altered, on pain of practical incoherence. The claim in the book is only that Hegel gives us the means for raising such a question with respect to a productive activity, art, purposely undertaken by a collective subject, Geist, over historical time, in effect our historical time. There is no guarantee such a retrospective teleological development can be defended. Such a claim can only be defended in the details. I try to do this. As Rush points out, post‐Hegel, we have to take account of the fact that there turned out not be the sort of social and philosophical reconciliation that Hegel thought would render art “a thing of the past.” Indeed, it now looks like the idea of the possibility of such a reconciliation is a kind of fantasy. But a failure to realize human freedom is not a failure in an all‐or‐nothing task. There are degrees and kinds of such a realization and degrees and kinds of failure at such a realization.12 If philosophy continues to have a historically diagnostic task, then there is no reason not to think that the production of art might remain indispensable in such diagnosis and critique.13 This issue of failed reconciliation is important in Adrian Daub's comments as well. There is a kind of appropriateness for this focus that goes beyond what he says explicitly. In my account the issue emerges in the treatment of Cézanne's three great Bather paintings and a threatened failure of sense more extreme than anything a “Hegelian” could imagine or account for. Indeed, it is not only persistent formal experimentations that evince some sense that conventional means of aesthetic expression cannot any longer achieve success (thereby manifesting a crisis in self‐understanding more extensive than the aesthetic), but a strain of dissatisfaction, negation, melancholy, and even nihilism would seem to raise the stakes considerably in any defense of the continuing relevance of a profoundly rationalist thinker like Hegel. These are issues that must be raised at a rather extreme level of abstraction, but my sense is that this commitment by Hegel to a form of rational reconciliation and the role of art in such a project is what is most at issue in Daub's Adorno‐inspired comments and so should be addressed explicitly as such. In other words, Manet and Cézanne are one thing; Wagner and eventually Schönberg or Berg, Kafka and Beckett and Eliot, and Rothko and Pollock are quite another. In that context, it would be understandable to place one's bet on a thinker for whom the essential task of modernist art is “negation,” a refusal of any implication in (complicity with) conventional sense‐making practices (and their implicit commitments), no matter what extreme, dissonant, difficult, or opaque means are necessary, someone like Theodor Adorno.14 For Daub, as I understand him, these latter considerations cast a shadow of sorts over Hegel's unusual position about the aesthetic idea, the beautiful, understood as the “sensible shining” of the aesthetic idea, the “identity of subject and  That is not merely a   It is a    such an  cannot be   Hegel seems to  an   to  development that   its realization only with the end of, the  of, art itself  the unusual claim that art  itself as art  in the   in  and has been      there is something  and  in this  something  to the aesthetic  to our embodiment and   that art   us in    to the  of    in the  These are all   and I think   Daub's  to  first, that Hegel's account cannot be  to a much   of modernist art,  it  cannot  Rush's “musical” modernism or  the  of the  with   itself in much of modernism,    Hegel's  ideal of a rational  of subject and  is  to art itself,  to    some  of   is a   As in the  I  in the  Hegel was the first to realize that the end of art is implicit in its  That his  was not  is   on his historical  He   by  the  as if it  the  of the    the   of the  of  art   to the  of reconciliation in the  of the  But what  means by the  of reconciliation will most  not involve the  of the    is the issue of   and my emphasis on  That is much more Hegel's  than his   of   in  to terms with these  a great  is  to  on the meaning of the  of  the   and the role of art in achieving one or manifesting the  Hegel's most  account of the  issue of relevance to art  in the  this way:   the    this  in  which makes  an    he now has to  in two  which  one another. title: Hegel, moderniste? Remarks on Robert Pippin's After the Beautiful
abstract: Robert Pippin's After the Beautiful presents a case for the continuing relevance of Hegel's aesthetic theory and of more broadly Hegelian approaches to the philosophy of art.1 As is characteristic of Pippin's work, the book is both illuminating and a rich source for further reflection. Pippin's case relies on restricting certain of Hegel's philosophical views, and the restrictions in question are not trivial. In particular, Hegel's claim that art no longer can have a leading or even significant role in increased human self‐understanding and in the realization of freedom must be set aside (pp. 35–39). Such negative pronouncements on the part of Hegel concerning art's continued viability for modern European self‐understanding simply have not stood the test of time. So, Pippin holds that, going forward, the Hegelian should treat such attitudes on the part of Hegel as extrusions of an overly strict, teleological conception of dialectic. One must liberate Hegelianism, that is, from the letter of Hegel's dialectic and so from his statements that art has ended—first, with respect to its role as a leading vehicle of human self‐knowledge in classical Greece and, second, in terms of its very ability to convey further self‐knowledge with romanticism. Divorcing dialectic from overarching teleology is in effect the only Hegelian thing to do if Hegel's dialectical conception of self‐determination (Selbstbestimmung) is to gain purchase in the discussion of modern art. More specifically Pippin is concerned to understand in Hegelian terms modern European painting roughly from the realism of Courbet and Manet to post‐impressionism. Pippin refers to this as a period of “pictorial modernism.” I take it that this phrase is to be understood as an abbreviated genitive that one should read both “subjectively” and “objectively.” That is, pictorial modernism is both the modernism of pictorial art (genitivus obiectivus = how modernism is expressed via the pictorial arts) and a specific kind of modernism (genitivus subiectivus = how modernism more generally is pictorial). Although Pippin does not quite come out and say it, After the Beautiful forwards a competitor to the mainstream way of charting the development of modern pictorial art (and other modern art as well) in terms of its increasing musicality. This conception of the development of art in the period under consideration, which one finds in different forms in Schelling, Schopenhauer, Wagner, Nietzsche, and Adorno, is a species of the Renaissance practice of paragone, taking the move from figural art to abstraction to be more indicative of what counts as “modern.” But it is not exactly silent on Pippin's favorite examples of French realism. It is important to note that the musicality hypothesis is compatible with certain aspects of Hegel's aesthetic progressivism, for instance, with the idea that one mode of art goads inferior modes into replicating imperfectly the advanced effects and structures of the superior mode. So, I am not sure Pippin wants to reject the musicality thesis outright and replace it with his concentration on pictorial modernism as a leading edge or whether he holds that they can complement one another. Prima facie the contrast between the two ways of thinking about modern art promises to be stark. For the musicality theorist the central concern is releasing subjectivity from the normative confines of the social and natural world through procedures of figural abstraction and summoning forth the Dionysian unconscious. The subjectivity primarily at issue here is not one pre‐adapted to sociality but rather one that increases its depth by radically restructuring reality in its own terms. This project has its clear antecedents in romanticism, as many scholars have recognized. In contrast, Pippin's Hegel will valorize realism—a position the historical Hegel would certainly have appreciated—and the idea of mutual recognition, not a breaking of the social vessels, is central. So, while Pippin is careful to restrict his specific case for the continuing relevance of Hegel's philosophy of art to the time period extending from what many art historians take to be the emergence of modern painting in Manet in the 1860s to the stirrings of figural abstraction in Cézanne's Bathers from the first decade of the twentieth century, there is even more at stake. Hegel of course did not live to see modern Europe. If one were to take as authoritative Hegel's statements at the conclusion of his lectures on aesthetics, one would not have much to go on in developing an account of modernism. One would be left with an extension of Dutch portraiture or with what Hegel calls in his treatment of poetry “true” or “objective” humor.2 It is my sense that Pippin takes his cue very much from the former. The latter is not a very exciting category by modernist lights.3 How one moves on from Hegel in a yet recognizably Hegelian vein raises questions both of (A) whether one can isolate sufficiently the results of the dialectic from the teleological dialectical apparatus and (B) if one can do so, which elements of dialectic one would feature going forward. I agree with Pippin that Hegel's own view generally is that Geist is in a position to certify to itself that it has achieved in principle full reconciliation with aspects of the world, it, and the relation of world to it, that were otherwise alienating. Hegel makes this claim for theoretical closure at a level of philosophical analysis that he considers much more advanced than the consideration of art—that is, at the level of the final and culminating form of what he calls “Absolute Spirit,” that is, “Philosophy.” “Art” is also a form of Absolute Spirit, one that is subordinate to Philosophy, and the impact of full reconciliation and theoretical closure on it follows from the subordination. Art's “end” for Hegel is, in that sense, a technical result internal to Hegel's theory of Absolute Spirit. Pippin does not argue for (A) above but finds himself in a long line of neo‐Hegelians in holding that releasing the teleological constraints of Hegel's own conception of dialectic as they operate at the overarching architectonic level does not present any special problem with preserving a recognizably Hegelian conception of dialectical rationality. He is also in neo‐Hegelian company in answering (B), in finding the conception of recognition to be a key to advancing “what lives,” as Croce put it, of Hegel.4 What is required to advance Hegel's views into modernity is a sense of recognition with ample room for alienation, that is, what one might call a Hegelian sense of failed recognition. And that is precisely what Pippin provides. Before one gets to the topic of recognition, two preliminary matters of reconstruction seem crucial for Pippin. The first is to preserve Hegel's historicism, especially as it intersects with another element of his thought: his rejection of a strict concept/percept division. Hegel treats the concept/percept binary contextually. The binary is theoretically permissible and even necessary and progressive given certain background assumptions. But if one were to ask whether ultimately there is a divide in theory or experience between categorial thought and cognitive receptivity, the answer for Hegel clearly would be that there is no such division. Second, Hegel analyzes action as a full‐fledged and, in many ways, basic form of thought. In particular, bodily action of forming objects is thinking, as is the bodily action of forming things whose main point is that they be seen as expressing the action constitutive of their making—for instance, art. It is worthwhile at this point to step back from Hegel's own doctrines in order to motivate via a more neutral medium how they might be extended in the artistic cases Pippin discusses. Hegel views art as inherently dealing in sensuously embedded concepts. That art is conceptual means that it is a form of Geist’s self‐expression and self‐knowledge; that it is sensuous is what makes it the form of Absolute Spirit that it is over and against other such forms. What is at issue here is visual art and sight; more specifically, what is at stake is how sight might be a form of conceptual life. Now, there is an approach to perception when it comes to considering sense modalities and their relation to more articulating modes of cognition that holds that sense modalities an sich and at their basic level are impervious to conceptual articulation. Sensuous perception on this account is passive in its receptivity, and whatever role it has in conceptually articulated experience is given to it “down the line” by higher order, conceptual modes of experience: one can and does (quite a lot of the time) see without thinking. But this is not the only approach to perception. One might instead argue that seeing is dependent on looking. To say that seeing is dependent on looking is to say that to see X one needs to orient one's sight with regard to X—that is, that seeing X requires an intentional action of bringing sight to X. Given this, one might informally summarize an argument for the ascription of recognition at a pre‐predicative or pre‐reflective level of visual experience as follows: Looking is an intentional activity, that is, one which operates even at the point of its minimal specification in terms of something like “choice.” Intentional activities, even at minimal levels of their specifications, are already cognitively structured and, so, are pre‐adapted to further structuring by intentional content of a more developed sort (for instance, beliefs). Seeing requires looking. Seeing is always intentional. Seeing, because intentional itself, is pre‐adapted to structuring in terms of more developed intentional content. I believe Hegel would accept something like this account of vision and its relation to looking and its inherent conceptual articulation, and I take it that Pippin would agree (pp. 41–42, 49–50). The conclusion of the argument is compatible with treating perception as embodied; Merleau‐Ponty is a kind of Hegelian in this sense. It is also compatible with treating the conceptual articulation of perceptual states as a matter of the concepts that are available for such structuring at different points in history. That said, it is easy to see that, while the argument establishes a potential basis for grafting the structure of Hegelian recognition to pre‐reflective visual states that form the basis for an aesthetic, sensuous dimension, by itself it is insufficient to do so. It is simply not specific enough. For one thing, from the fact that seeing involves looking and from the fact that looking involves at least some minimal sense of regard for the thing looked at, one cannot draw any immediate conclusion concerning whether such regard will be positive, negative, or in between. Even assuming that what is looked at is another looker, that does not without more entail that the regard is a kind of recognition, which in the Hegelian vein is certainly not neutral and in most cases operates according to at least a tacit ideal of positive mutual regard. (Of course, in some of the most famous of his cases, Hegel attempts to show that mutual antagonistic regard is the product of at least the stirrings of, say, respect.) Nor does the conclusion of the argument entail that the regard, be it positive or negative, would provide an impetus to sustained interaction between one who is looking, on the one hand, and what or whom is being looked at, on the other. That the thing looked at is itself a looker also does not guarantee this result without more said about the relation of looking, the nature of lookers, or both. But here again it seems that ordinary experience can help the Hegelian out a bit, for looking and being looked at do seem to be basically experientially and conceptually interrelated. Soon after a child can look she is aware that she can be looked at, and this awareness infiltrates and forms her looking in terms of her being looked at. This is a signal structure for the Hegelian, as Pippin emphasizes, for the reciprocity of seeing qua looking now can be further specified in terms of recognition and its application to at least visual art that makes the combination of looking and being looked at thematic, and some modernist visual art clearly has that brief. For, once one allows that seeing has intentional structure ab initio, it is open to one to argue that this intentional base can be modeled in various sorts of personal, social, and historical ways by interpenetrating conceptual resources. That is, the idea of intention here plays a structural role within an account of perception that facilitates what one might call the reciprocal ‘travel’ of cognitive resources from the more generically articulated to the less and from the less to the more. As Pippin writes in the introductory sections of the book, this picture is implied but not very well worked out by Kant (pp. 9–15); Hegel's epistemology makes it central by emphasizing the importance of the historical constitution of such resources.5 Of course, none of this structure uniquely supports the progressive historical story Hegelians often tell about such resources or the idea that reconciliation is always a tacit ideal of recognition. Hegelians will have to argue for the merits of those ideas independently. This is the point at which recognition can reenter the story. Ordinarily recognition is an explicit and fully conceptual action; one would not ordinarily say that seeing without more involves the sort of regard that typifies Hegelian recognition. “Recognition” is a social–moral category for him that, if it has work to do at the perceptual/sensuous level, will involve various relatively conceptually inarticulate ways of looking and being looked at. Take Manet's Olympia. The painting is both a mediation and provocation concerning canons of looking at nudes. The titular figure looks at one looking at her as a nude; her look says, depending on one's interpretation, “what are you looking at?” “what are you looking at?” or “why are looking at all?”6 Her look defies that of the onlooker, thereby placing in question the art‐historical project of making objects that solicit the kinds of looking that female nudes typically do. T. J. Clark's treatment of the Olympia and of other of Manet's works strikes me as especially convincing.7 As Clark sees things, the painting is in dialogue with both the historical practice of painting nudes (compare Manet's reference to Titian's Venus of Urbino) as well as with the “low” material culture of its day. Michael Fried has argued that one such source is the contemporary practice of photographing prostitutes for pornographic purposes.8 Alexander Nehamas extends the point in holding that the painting is of such a photographic session.9 Nehamas's more explicit reference to photography overreaches; it is more plausible and powerful to view Manet's painting as painting not of a photographic session but under the aesthetic style of such photography, as Fried suggests. Nevertheless, concentration on photography as a normative presence in the work is brilliant in unmasking the particular kind of pretention that Olympia's look foregrounds. Its focus on the encroachment of exchange relations (prostitutes, pornographic postcards) into easel painting is of a piece with Clark's insistence that, if one looks hard enough at scenes of middle‐ and lower middle‐class leisure painted in impressionism, one sees factories and other modes of advancing industrialization. For Clark, the appeal to “flatness” that features, say, in Greenberg's account of abstract expressionism and Fry's of post‐impressionism gains in social weight in Manet's case; the flatness of the canvas is a very specific sort—the flatness of such photographs. One tries to look at Olympia under the duplicitous guise of the nude—as if looking at her were anything but buying her for erotic use. Her look at that looking—the way being looked at is directed back at the audience—disabuses one of the fiction. She does not merely look at or past one; rather she looks through one. title: State of Play: Visual Culture and Music
abstract: The Music of Painting: Music, Modernism and the Visual Arts from the Romantics to John Cage, by Peter, Vergo, London: Phaidon Press Ltd, 2010, 368pp., hbk, 16 col. and 230 b. & w. illus., $89.95, £39.95 Music and Modernism, c. 1849–1950, edited by Mille Charlotte, Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing, 2011, hbk, 355pp., 69 b. & w. illus., £44.99 Art as Music, Music as Poetry, Poetry as Art, from Whistler to Stravinsky and Beyond, by Peter, Dayan, Farnham: Ashgate, 2011, 190pp., hbk, 8 col. and 5 b. & w. illus., £55.00 The publication of these three books provides an opportunity to review what we can now confidently call a true field of research: music and visual culture. It may not exactly have come of age, but it is at least up and running as a scholarly endeavour producing ever more lively, challenging and substantial research. These publications represent rather different faces of the subject, asking in the way of Gauguin: ‘Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?’ But they may also indicate an answer to these questions. The Music of Painting by Peter Vergo addresses the first question and functions as a touchstone in this endeavour. Vergo has been interested in the relationships between music and the visual arts for over thirty years and was one of the first voices in the field.1 The collection edited by Charlotte de Mille is a ‘state of play’ (‘what are we’) selection of essays, mainly by early career scholars, that displays a refreshing range of approaches and research topics; a clear portrait of the field's complex and polyphonic identity. Peter Dayan's book is a series of related case studies that, nevertheless, provoke a bold, over-arching theoretical ambition. The ability to formulate a coherent theoretical project is, I hope, indicative of where research in the field needs to go. Vergo's The Music of Painting is a sequel to his earlier study That Divine Order: Music and the Visual Arts from Antiquity to the Eighteenth Century (also published by Phaidon, in 2005) and together they represent a kind of summa of these interests. They provide a survey of art and music relations, from Western antiquity and ancient Chinese music and art theory, to the career of the American composer John Cage in the middle of the twentieth century. That Divine Order largely focused on mathematical order and music, positing harmony, via music, as a paradigm that might be adopted by artists seeking to claim a value for their own art that some felt it might otherwise lack. However, The Music of Painting is both textually longer (by nearly one hundred pages) and chronologically shorter in scope. It also has a less clearly articulated thesis; unlike That Divine Order, mathematical order is engaged in only as a small part of the story of twentieth-century art, and the concept of harmony, central to the earlier book, underwent a revolutionary transformation during the timeframe engaged by this second book, through (but not exclusively) the impact of Schoenberg and then the aleatoric aesthetics of his pupil John Cage. Vergo is at his best when setting out his stall, when discussing paintings that aspire to musical principles, or explaining basic music theory and how it does, or does not, inform painterly aspirations. Both That Divine Order and The Music of Painting provide a treasure trove of empirical material and detail. To take two exactly contemporary examples from the latter: Vergo is fascinating on the construction of Vladimir Baranoff-Rossiné's ‘optophonic piano’ (1923), and compelling in his argument that Paul Klee's painting New Harmony (1936) is unlikely to have been directly influenced by Schoenberg's dodecaphonic interests (despite the views of earlier commentators).2 Vergo argues that it is closely related formally and colourwise to Klee's own Intensification of Colour from Static to Dynamic of 1923. This work was painted around the same time that the Second Viennese School were privately discussing Schoenberg's ‘Method of Composing with Twelve Tones which are related only with one another’3 and, therefore, too early for a more general public awareness (plate 1). In the forward ‘Towards the Condition of Music’, Vergo writes ‘I have largely ignored Cage's attempts to incorporate into the domain of music not merely silence but also indeterminate sounds and noises’ (6). My position would be different: I would see silence and indeterminate sounds and noises as always and already part of all music. What Cage did was simply to shift emphasis, to show that there is no silence anyway, and that indeterminacy in composition is supplemented by determinacy in performance (and vice versa). This is why the phrase ‘Cage's silent piano piece’ (as the dust jacket has it) is not a very helpful way of describing 4’33” - it is not silent, nor necessarily a piano piece, nor indeed fixed at 4 minutes and 33 seconds! In addition, what silence and noise (as concepts or aspirations, if not as sonoric absences or facts) bring to music is an opportunity to explore music's ontology, and it is here, I would argue, that the visual is located. As with silence and indeterminacy, the visual is already present, if often undetected in the shadows. This conceptual difference apart, I also differ from Vergo in his assertion that ‘electronic music, multimedia installation, video art and other developments’ are ‘part of a different story’ (6), hence his reluctance to include them in the present study. In many ways the story he tells of art and music in the twentieth century is one of aspiration foiled by technology. Alexander Laszlo's ‘colour-light’ performances, Hans Richter's, Viking Eggeling's or Oskar Fischinger's ‘visual music’ films, Moholy-Nagy's interest in the gramophone as a creative instrument rather than simply a reproductive one; all of these experiments would find fuller incarnation as the century wore on: in John Whitney's films and his ‘analog computer’ during his time as artist in residence at IBM in the mid-1960s; in the work of artists associated with Fluxus, especially an artist like Nam June Paik who subverted technologies of reproduction via techniques of feedback; or in the more contemporary work of VJ artists such as Addictive TV who ran the visual music event Optronica in London in 2005–07 (see http://www.addictive.com/), or the audio-visual remix act Eclectic Method who also sample, mix and re-edit audio-visual material, both in live performance and in audio and video recordings (see http://www.eclecticmethod.net/). Vergo's story stops in the 1960s just as technology arrives at a point where the idea of visual music can be more fully realized. Indeed, in the decade following Vergo's cut-off point, multimedia experimentation really starts to take off. © Paul Klee/DACS, London 2010/Bridgeman Art Library However, my main critical point about The Music of Painting is not what is included and what is not – one can always find other examples and practitioners – nor where the chronological bounds have been drawn (his project to cover antiquity to the mid-twentieth century is already more ambitious that most other researchers in the field). My main point of critique is in relation to issues of theory. Vergo makes the following point in his introduction: ‘I have dismissed any idea of trying to apply methods borrowed from some pre-existing body of theory to the extremely diverse source material considered here’ (7). While this does commendable justice to the individual works discussed, it does not provide any sense, or explanation, regarding what lay beneath all the efforts to speak across media. It is precisely this that Dayan attempts to do. The distinctions between interplay at the level of multi-, inter- or cross-mediality is not explicitly explored, although it is implicitly engaged in some examples. Vergo is especially good at explaining the technical differences between media, what musical concepts mean and how they can or cannot be ‘transferred’ across media. What is less convincing is the interrogation of this very idea of ‘transferal’ or ‘translation,’ and on this Dayan has interesting things to say. To take cubism as one more example from Vergo: as he correctly points out, ‘one remarkable feature of their works [Picasso's and Braque's] painted between about 1909 and 1914 is the prevalence of musical subject matter. This can sometimes account for more than fifty percent of their still-life paintings in any given year’, and he goes on to say that this may appear surprising ‘given their repeated denials that they knew or understood anything at all about painting's sister art’. However, the analysis of this tantalizing issue stops at the admission that, ‘no matter how poetically adapted or even distorted such depictions might turn out to be’, Picasso and Gris ‘were in some cases painting objects that first met their gaze’ (214–15). Braque is discussed in a little more detail, but the discussion soon moves on to more formal issues of space and time, and never returns to attempt an answer to the question of why music was so ubiquitous (plate 2). There is no discussion of, for example, the relationship between such still lives and the trompe l'oeil tradition with which they so clearly engage, and which likewise drew on musical subject matter for reasons of sensory play (invoking touch, as musical instruments must), in addition to raising questions fundamental to issues of representation and illusion, dear to the hearts of cubists.4 Nor does Vergo discuss the relationship between the references to music and other collage elements in synthetic cubism. The reading of the newspaper elements of many of these works, by Robert Rosenblum and Patricia Leighten among numerous others, has raised issues about the relationship between content and subject matter and the complex dialectics set up at various levels of signification within and without the work.5 Vergo missed the opportunity to weave this debate into the role of music as the principle subject of many of these collages.6 Music is an ideal paradigm for the way in which signification can float free of fixed signifiers, and as such it provided Picasso with a means of play (jouer or jouir): he made poetry out of the public discourse of current events played out in the pages of Le Journal. Indeed, given how important the artists involved in this movement are (more so than, say, Henrik Neugeboren who takes up almost as much space a few pages further on), they occupy surprisingly little of Vergo's overall story. © Georges Braque/ADAGP, Paris and DACS, London 2010 So while Vergo's book is a mine of practical connections, artists, works and ideas, it does not provide a wider sense of orientation or theoretical context: how do notions of the modern play out against the ideology of media mixture, for example? Central to any attempt to answer this is the necessity to engage theories of modernism. I have been especially interested in exploring the drive to media exclusivity marked by Clement Greenberg's theory of modernism, for example, how it is built on the model of music, and how the contrary synthetic impulse to media hybridity constantly plays against this more purist paradigm. Like Vergo, Dayan does not explicitly engage this corpus of ideas, but he does a parallel job. De Mille's collection, on the other hand, is emphatically and explicitly engaged with modernity and, according to the dust jacket, aims to ‘re-think modernism itself in the light of both the fine arts and music, to advocate a multiplicity of modernisms…’. Her book has been sensibly selected, edited and designed, from a series of papers given at a Royal Musical Association conference in March 2008, and is organized in five sections with an introductory essay by Vergo. The quality of the essays, as in any collection, varies, but they are rarely less than interesting and often innovative in the insights they offer. The majority are by scholars early in their engagement in the field, demonstrating thoughtful, careful and detailed analysis of a gratifyingly diverse range of approaches and case studies. The first section considers German aesthetics, especially the legacy of Wagner's much-misunderstood concept of the Gesamtkunstwerk. The accounts range from Diane Silverthorne's essay on music and book design in the Vienna Secession, to Spyros Petritakis's comparison of Richard Strauss's compositional interests and Böcklin's art in the context of German nationalism. Isabel Wünsche's essay closes this section and considers synaesthesia and the early twentieth-century Russian artists Nikolai Kulbin and Wassily Kandinsky, as well as the composer Mikhail Matyushin. The concept of synaesthesia, together with that of the Gesamtkunstwerk, both introduced in this first part, are so important that they stray into other sections of the book. Indeed, the first essay in the second section is on French art and the Gesamtkunstwerk in the late nineteenth century: Jim Rubin writes on Wagner's ideas and the evocation of sound in Courbet's landscapes, whilst Corrinne Chong's essay on the aesthetics of vagueness, an attribute associated with signification in instrumental music, considers Fantin-Latour and Berlioz. The third section has two essays, one by Ayla Lepine, which provides an account of English ecclesiastical architecture in Cambridge and spiritualism read through the multi-medial and sensory nature of such spaces, and the editor's own essay. De Mille offers a neat account of the conflation of German expressionism and Bloomsbury's aesthetic concerns through specific writings by Virginia Woolf and Kandinsky. Section four links early abstract animated films in Malcolm Cook's essay with Jody Patterson's account of Stuart Davis’ paintings, jazz and the political left in New Deal America. The final section has two essays on mid-century topics: Melissa Warak's account of the Fluxus works of La Monte Young and their relationship to Zen ideas, and a consideration by Olga Touloumi of Xenakis and Le Corbusier's Philips Pavilion for the World Fair of 1958, the importance of drawing, and the graphic and mathematical elements of musical scoring. This should give some sense of the scope of this collection, and while the sectioning of the essays is not always entirely convincing, nor the book's title, which gives no indication of the comparative nature of the enterprise, the book does provide a collective indication of the riches to be mined from a rigorous consideration of the visual culture of music. While de Mille's book may be polyphonic, it does, like Vergo's, leave the difficult, complex, but ultimately perhaps most stimulating and interesting questions, to one side. This is perhaps inevitable with a collection of essays, but the answers to which we should perhaps now turn are to be discovered by seeking out the ‘thorough bass’ of music–art relationships. I evoke Goethe here, in a quote familiar to all who work in this area. In conversation with his assistant Riemer on 19 May 1807, Goethe pointed to a lack of an underlying theory in art: ‘Painting has long since lacked knowledge of any Generalbass; it lacks any accepted theory as exists in music.’7 Basso continuo, as it is perhaps more commonly known, is a means of realizing harmony based on bass notes alone (sometimes with figures, hence ‘figured bass’). The relevant point is that the rules of continuo realization are widely enough understood to allow a skilled player to realize the harmony from an unfigured bass part. Goethe's remark was about the lack of an intuitively felt, but objectively understood, theoretical harmonic foundation. This point was later picked up by Kandinsky and seen by him as both a plea for a comprehensive artistic theory (for abstraction in art) and one based after the model of music theory (the most abstract of the fine arts) (plate 3). I do not propose the construction of an essentialist theory of music–art relations, but believe attempts to dig beneath the surface, to seek out ideological coincidences, and to construct interdisciplinary connections, as Dayan's book does, should be sought out and applauded when attempted. © Wassily Kandinsky/ADAGP, Paris and DACS, London 2010 Whilst the title of Dayan's book says it all and makes for intelligibility, it is rather clunky, distinctly unmemorable, and, since the image on the front makes the same point as the title by other means, the overall design is rather cluttered. Dayan's case studies are well chosen: two artists, two composers and two poets; James Abbot McNeill Whistler, Erik Satie, Guillaume Apollinaire, Georges Braque, Francis Ponge and Igor Stravinsky. They form discrete, but complementary instances which allow Dayan to develop and nuance his argument effectively. This is an interesting book, and one that comes from outside the usual field of references. It is refreshing, despite the relative youth of the field, to have common questions considered from different angles. It does, of course, have an impact on the originality of the arguments; many of Dayan's establishing points ‘feel’ familiar if couched in different words, yet his conclusions are often refreshingly new. What Dayan means, for example, by ‘an interart aesthetic’ is what could also be described as a central plank of many theories of modernism; Daniel Albright, to pick an example almost at random, shares points of reference with Dayan, but his work is not mentioned.8 Indeed, Dayan shares hardly any common references with the other two books reviewed (his chronology is similar, but his geography is more restricted). In addition, unlike the other books, Dayan sets out to establish laws on which to construct his argument. Its core argument, with which I have a great deal of sympathy, is this: from the end of the nineteenth century to the middle of the twentieth, an intermedial aesthetic principle was established by which artistic value was to be sought, not within the formal logic of the unique medium, but through the transposed value of another medium. Thus art is judged as music, music as poetry and poetry as art. The key issue here is that music, poetry and art are to be understood as aspirations separate from specific manifestations. Thus, there is no question of a particular work of art being judged as if it ‘illustrated’ a particular piece of music; rather, painting as an art aspires to the condition of music. This is obviously not an original argument, but where it does diverge from Walter Pater's dynamic is in the circular nature of this field of references.9 So art is not to be grounded in music, rather, music then slips into the aspiration of the  which then  to the value of  This   is a   for discussing issues of  especially in the   on the  of an interart aesthetic together with a  interest in   in the contemporary art of Richard  and   Dayan    and the    that we have no  to the  laws of art. title: The New Woman and the ekphrastic poetics of Bela Balazs
abstract: Film studies has long acknowledged the centrality to the discipline of the female subject as historical protagonist, symbolic representation and theoretical construct. My contribution to this dossier suggests, however, that there remains work to be done on the relation between early film theory and early twentieth-century femininity. Femininity, more pointedly, can be considered from both a historical and a symbolic standpoint as a structuring element within early film theory. I elaborate this argument here in a discussion of the early writings of Béla Balázs: specifically of the two interwar treatises, Visible Man (1924) and The Spirit of Film (1930), in which Balázs explored the part played by film and cinematic perception in the formation of new social subjects. As Balázs wrote in The Spirit of Film, ‘the substrate of [the film medium's] development is the subject, the human subject, man in his social being’.1 After his turn to Marxism towards the end of World War I, Balázs's primary commitment was to the working class as that ‘subject … in his social being’ who was destined to become the collective agent of historical change. Yet his own life trajectory suggests the significance for Balázs of a second emergent historical protagonist: the New Woman, whom we know from feminist history to have become by the turn of the century a second global agent of social, economic and cultural change.2 Political feminism was formative for Balázs: he wrote an early essay on feminism, and worked alongside feminist activists in the short-lived Budapest Commune of 1919. He nurtured lifelong and intellectually formative relationships with women artists and intellectuals, among them Anna Lesznai, the writer and illustrator who helped to shape Balázs's thinking on cinema as a fairy-tale mass popular art, as I discuss below.3 Similarly ubiquitous in Balázs's early writings are references to the popular female stars who embodied the New Woman's emancipatory ideals as well as her frustrated desires – Lilian Gish, Pola Negri, Suzanne Desprès and, most famously, Asta Nielsen. But the New Woman's pervasive presence in Balázs's writing is not yet matched by a full understanding of her heuristic significance as image and female muse. In what follows, I therefore take Balázs's writings on female star performance as a point of entry for a discussion of the generative – because, I suggest, ekphrastic – relation in which his film theory stands to the New Woman as image, cinema icon and myth. Balázs concludes Visible Man with an encomium to Nielsen, the star long recognized by cinema historians as a key figure in early twentieth-century cinema's articulation of the New Woman myth. But Balázs's debt to her goes further. At the close of Visible Man he situates Nielsen and Charlie Chaplin as early silent cinema's emblematic stars, presenting them as exemplifying in their performance and star persona what he considers to be the specific aesthetic properties of the film medium. Their juxtaposition reveals the gendered vision on which Balázs's film theory rests. Reiterating his plea from the book's introduction that film be recognized as the quintessential modern art form, Balázs writes of Chaplin that his is a ‘popular art in the best sense’, a form of ‘modern American folk poetry’ whose stories redeem a ‘reified, mechanized society’ by recasting it within a ‘poetry of ordinary life, the inarticulate life of ordinary things’. Chaplin's silent performances of the ‘little guy’ in the American city thus embody for Balázs a collective poetics: the mute visual poetry of everyday life in the modern urban mass (pp. 85–86). Nielsen's function is quite different. Richard Dyer long ago identified as a key feature of stardom its ambivalent fusion in a single personality of the ordinary and the extraordinary. Stars, according to Dyer, project an image that is both ‘special’ and ‘spectacular’, but are also known, through their screen roles as well as celebrity chatter, as emblems of the familiar everyday.4 Balázs's Visible Man epilogue does not, however, reproduce the conjunction between the ordinary and the extraordinary that Dyer identifies within individual stars. Instead it divides those qualities along gender lines, operating with a distinction that places Chaplin on the side of ‘ordinary life … ordinary things’, and Nielsen in the elevated realm of what Dyer calls the extraordinary but which might also be termed the modern sublime. Balázs's ecstatic prose certainly recalls Romantic adorations of the sublime when he declaims: Just as we are tempted to despair that film can ever be capable of becoming a genuine form of art on its own, an art worthy of being represented by a tenth Muse on Mount Olympus; just as we are on the verge of accepting that film can never be more than a lame version of theatre … Asta Nielsen … restor[es] our faith and our conviction. … lower the flags in her honour, she is incomparable and without peer. (pp. 87–88) Nielsen's first claim to Olympian status derives from her command of this new ‘gesturology’. Her performances are, for Balázs, ‘stupefying’ in their ‘diversity’, their ‘wealth of mimed expressions’ and their rootedness in the vast ‘thesaurus of gestures’ on which she alone can draw (p. 87). Her second triumph resides in an ‘erotic charisma’ that makes manifest the film medium's status as the early twentieth century's emblematic secular art. As Dyer further reminds us, the prestige of the cinema star derives from historical processes of cultural modernization that have unseated ancient gods, replacing them with secular deities including the idols of the silver screen.5 The idea of film spectatorship as a secular version of a sacred quest is confirmed when Balázs notes that Nielsen's performances establish the erotic as ‘film's very own theme, its essence’ (p. 87). Here, then, the search for a blissful union with the godhead is replaced by erotic desires for the body of a desired other on screen. But the ‘mute understanding’ that arises from this erotic union derives for Balázs, thirdly, from a play of performed expressions exemplified not only in Nielsen's expressive body but in her face. Studies of Balázs regularly identify the face both as a key figure in his analyses of screen performance and as a founding metaphor in a Balázsian phenomenology attentive to the ‘physiognomy of things’.6 Equally familiar is Balázs's celebration of the facial closeup as the ‘poetry of the cinema’: a ‘mute pointing’ that expresses within the duration of a single shot an ‘entire view of life’ (pp. 39–41). That Nielsen's performance represents once again for Balázs the quintessence of this cinematic poetry is confirmed when he celebrates her ability to do ‘what children do’, which is to wear ‘not only her own expression but, barely noticeably (although we always sense it), the expression of her interlocutor, which is reflected as in a mirror. … She carries the entire dialogue in her features and fuses it into a synthesis of understanding and experiencing’ (p. 88). Nielsen's screen image functions in Visible Man, then, as both visual foil and affective trigger for a gendered film-critical account that locates the female body on screen as the source of a quintessentially cinematic erotic power. Balázs's reflections, moreover, are couched not in the rationalist abstraction of, say, a new film grammar but in an ekphrastic poetics that both acknowledges and disavows the feminine autonomy for which Nielsen's image stands. Ekphrasis – a term deriving from classical rhetoric, and defined in that context as an ‘elaborate digressive disruption [in] rhetorical discourse’ – has recently attracted the attention of literary scholars seeking critical concepts adequate to the literary arts on an image-saturated age. Stephen Cheeke, for instance, observes that the contemporary ‘immersion of poets in the “image world”’ has produced a ‘corresponding struggle to render or control the image verbally’, a struggle he explores in an illuminating study of ekphrastic poetry from the Renaissance to the present day.7 But Cheeke's final chapter, an essay on ‘prose ekphrasis’, suggests that the term – which for him has purchase on art history and criticism from Goethe, Johann Winckelmann and Gotthold Lessing to Walter Benjamin – may also help illuminate the relation between the moving image and its rerendering in the effusive critical prose of Balázs. Visible Man was written well in advance of any properly institutionalized film theory or criticism. Drawing substantially on reviews for the Vienna daily Der Tag – the first Austrian newspaper to employ, in the person of Balázs, a fully fledged film critic – the text shares with cognate works including Jean Epstein's Bonjour, Cinéma (1921) and Ricciotto Canudo's The Birth of the Sixth Art (1911) an experimental prose style that owes more to contemporary modernisms than to the realist epistemology of, say, linguistic or semiotic modes of film interpretation and critique. Though Balázs cites comparative linguistics as a possible model for a ‘gesturology’ of screen performance (p. 97), his own writing only begins to emulate that discipline's realist idiom in the formal grammar that he attempts in his 1930 Spirit of Film. Visible Man, by contrast, is notable for, among other features, its stylistic borrowings from expressionism, including second-person address (the ‘May we come in?’ of the prologue) and a mood or voice that is typically declarative, exclamatory, interrogative or even imperative, as in the ‘I have to tell you … you must’ of his opening demand to aestheticians that film be accorded ‘a chapter … in the great aesthetic systems’ (p. 3). In his influential theorization of the relation between film criticism or theory and the screen image, Christian Metz notes ‘the broadly projective character of the relation the cinema writer often maintains to his [sic] object’. Recognizing the generative function of film criticism – its productive capacity in relation to cinematic meaning and affect – Metz famously dubs film writing ‘the cinema's third machine’: an engine of textual production, then, that is fuelled by the desire of the critic to maintain a ‘good object relation’ with the medium of film. In Metz's Lacanian account, the cinema figures as a ‘technique of the imaginary … the definitive imprint of a stage before the Oedipus complex [and of] the exclusive relation to the mother’. What he calls cinematic writing is based in an initial move on ‘idealization’: the critic falls in love with the film, and produces writing that, in its crudest form, subsists in discourse only as fantasy, ‘an uninterpreted dream’.8 The move into film theory proper, however, demands an Oedipal separation from this maternal imaginary; thus the film writer must follow the Law of the Father by ‘break[ing] the beneficial image’, and striving after that ‘necessarily sadistic’ distance from its object which is the prerequisite for a fully elaborated theory of the film.9 Although Metz never advocates a cinema writing that abjures the critic's early love of cinema and film – we must, he writes, not lose sight of the cinephile, even while we strive ‘no longer [to] be invaded by him’ – he certainly repudiates those forms of early cinema theory that maintain film ‘in the imaginary enclosure of a pure love’.10 His rebuke surely extends to Balázs, whose stylistic excess in his early writings is evocative as much of their author's cinematic passions as of any objectified reality of the moving image in film. But work by Cheeke and others on ekphrasis suggests a possible recasting of Metz. Ekphrastic writing certainly recognizes the same otherness of the pictorial object that, for Metz, fuels film-critical desire. But it strives to overcome this through a poetic emulation that is in psychic terms more akin to mimesis – a mode of embodied identification that blurs self–other distinctions – than to the objectifying symbolizations of Metz's account. Ekphrasis, in other words, borrows from its visual object those aesthetic features that are also the signal characteristics of poetry, adopting a tone, rhythm, imagery and lyrical voice that perform an imaginary mirroring of the moving image on film. One instance from Balázs is his account of associational montage, whose rhythmic qualities he mimics when he describes it as flowing ‘smoothly and in a broad stream, like the hexameter in a classical epic, or else like a ballad, flaring up breathlessly and then … rising inexorably towards a climax, or tingling capriciously’ (pp. 3, 80). This is just one of numerous ekphrases in Balázs that reproduce the poetic textures of their critical object: here, associational montage; elsewhere, camera and the closeup, screen performance, colour or sound. This film-critical mimesis differs in important ways from the ‘third machine’ of Metz's account. Mimesis is distinguished in psychic terms from object relations in the Lacanian symbolic by the reciprocity of the relationship it establishes between self and other – or, in the present context, between critic and image on screen. Ekphrasis as a rhetorical practice is mimetic, therefore, not just by virtue of its stylistic impersonation of the image. As W. J. T. Mitchell observes, the sensuous dance that ekphrasis performs with its object also suggests an understanding of the image as ‘a thing that is always already addressing us … a subject with a life that has to be seen as “its own” in order for our descriptions to engage the picture's life as well as our own lives as beholders’.11 Mitchell's account is persuasive in the case of Balázs, whose phenomenological understanding of film as a material embodiment of modern experience indeed leads him to recognize the medium as ‘a subject with a life’ (pp. 67, 46). Hence his exaltation of fluid montage as film's ‘living breath’, or of the moving image as a vital expression of the ‘physiognomy of things’.
